body:
@sgugger 

Just realized this, here `labels` is a list but we need a `tensor` for `prepare_decoder_input_ids_from_labels` method. And can't turn that into a tensor here since it's not padded.

Thinking more about this, I would say we remove the `ignore_pad_token_for_loss` argument, this is rather a confusing name. In the previous script, it was used to specify that we should ignore pad tokens as it is (by setting the `ignore_index` in loss to `pad_token_id` ) rather than replacing them with -100 (because of the label smoothing issues). So in any case the pad tokens were ignored, and I don't think there is any reason to not ignore them.

So IMO we should 
- remove the `ignore_pad_token_for_loss` argument
- set `padding` to `True` when `pad_to_max_length` is False
- replace pad with -100 in the pre-processing function
- and remove/deprecate  the `DataCollatorForSeq2Seq`
author: patil-suraj

body:
> set padding to True when pad_to_max_length is False

This will pad to the maximum length of the batches sent to the map method of the dataset, not the maximum length of a batch, so this does not work. `DataCollatorForSeqSeq` is needed until we have the datasets v2 release to do that padding as a transform on the dataset (soon!) but we can't deprecate it just now.

body:
Again not familiar with TF way of working, but the actual inputs in PT do change quite a bit the actual traced graph.

That means that `use_cache` graph vs `first_pass` graph look quite different. Also setting variable seq_length where it can be fixed (for instance input_ids is necessarily [B, 1] for `use_cache` graph on decoder) can link to greatly different performance later down the road.

What I'm trying to say is that this test will probably check that the Ops used in TF are valid for some ONNX opset, **it does not by any means that check it can/will export the best production ready graph.**

And the real hot path in production is almost always, decoder-only with `use_cache` (even input_ids [1, 1]) within a generation loop (I don't think TF has the generation loop optimized yet.)

These are 2 different things.

1. in the case of DeepSpeed this is a clean cut. We explicitly init all these at the beginning of `train`:
https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/blob/22a32cf48527ee679dc538ba47e08a9d5c844dc2/src/transformers/trainer.py#L765-L771

body:
Thanks a lot for your PR! I have left a lot of comments but most of them are around styling and can actually be solved by one command to run on your side (see below). Here are some more general recommendations before we can merge:

1. **Example:** The example only works for IBert, therefore it should not be using the `Auto` classes but `IBert` classes, to get an error if the user provides a checkpoint that doesn't correspond to an ibert model. It should also be put in `examples/research_projects` as it's not one of the maintained examples tested by our CI.
2. **Utils organization:** I think the file in the utils submodule should be grouped in one `modeling_ibert_utils` or `quantization_utils` file directly inside the `ibert` folder. `quant_modules` uses everything that is inside `quant_utils` so there is no point in the separation and we usually want everything in one file.
3. **Formatting:** The formatting is not consistent with ours, and I left lots of comments on lines with `\`. The good news is that it will all be fixed if you just run `make style` on your branch.

This is debattable.

Are the proposition single tokens for mask tokens, or are they tuples of answers. Consider the following:

`This <mask> is to <mask> what rice is to sushi.`

Here are the top-3 proposition for the 3 masks:
[apple, rhubarb, Paris]
[pie, France, biking]

With your code, you are going to propose IIUC
(apple, pie)
(rhubarb, France)
(Paris, biking)

It's possible (not necessarely though) that the propositions you want to make are more like:

(apple, pie)
(rhubarb, pie)
(Paris, France).

My suggestion at this point it to look at joint probabilities for the tuple suggestion instead of token per token.

body:
I don't think you can do correct joint probabilities.
The output is **by design** the sum of all joint probabilities at every locus.
What I meant is Bert *cannot* outptut {token1:"either", token2:"or", score:50%}, {token1:"or", token2:"either", score:50%}. It *has* to output {token1: ["either", 50%], ["or", 50%]} {token2: ["either", 50%], ["or", 50%]}. So you have no way of recovering the first proposed solution and your best guess can only be (either either, 25), (either, or, 25), (or, either, 25), (or, or, 25) 

What I was suggesting, as a better guess, was simply treating them like they were:

- Softmax all mask locus independantly
- create all joint probabilities (lazily because it's a combinatorial)
  - p1_1 x p2_1
  - p1_1 x p2_2
  - ...
  - p1_2 x p2_1
  - ....
  - px_y where x is the location of the max token, and y is the rank of the proposed token
- Softmax that joint probabilities list (just so that output scores are correctly scaled, could be ignored because of combinatorial)
- Order them

body:
Agreed with @Narsil that we should handle backwards compatibility as much as possible here. Having a different return according to the number of masks isn't super clean but it's definitely way better than breaking the workflow of existing `fill-mask` pipeline users.

Pipelines are, by design, already a bit "magical", in the sense that it returns different outputs according to your inputs. If you pass the pipeline a string or a list of strings, the resulting type will be different:

```py
>>> from transformers import pipeline
>>> mask_filler = pipeline("fill-mask")
>>> mask_filler("Where do <mask> live?")
[{'sequence': '<s>Where do you live?</s>', 'score': 0.575425386428833, 'token': 47, 'token_str': 'Ġyou'}, {'sequence': '<s>Where do YOU live?</s>', 'score': 0.1382409781217575, 'token': 10540, 'token_str': 'ĠYOU'}, {'sequence': '<s>Where do they live?</s>', 'score': 0.044609859585762024, 'token': 51, 'token_str': 'Ġthey'}, {'sequence': '<s>Where do we live?</s>', 'score': 0.0327814482152462, 'token': 52, 'token_str': 'Ġwe'}, {'sequence': '<s>Where do millennials live?</s>', 'score': 0.02294538915157318, 'token': 15100, 'token_str': 'Ġmillennials'}]
>>> mask_filler(["Where do <mask> live?", "Where <mask> I live?"])
[[{'sequence': '<s>Where do you live?</s>', 'score': 0.5754269361495972, 'token': 47, 'token_str': 'Ġyou'}, {'sequence': '<s>Where do YOU live?</s>', 'score': 0.1382400244474411, 'token': 10540, 'token_str': 'ĠYOU'}, {'sequence': '<s>Where do they live?</s>', 'score': 0.044610150158405304, 'token': 51, 'token_str': 'Ġthey'}, {'sequence': '<s>Where do we live?</s>', 'score': 0.032781537622213364, 'token': 52, 'token_str': 'Ġwe'}, {'sequence': '<s>Where do millennials live?</s>', 'score': 0.022945256903767586, 'token': 15100, 'token_str': 'Ġmillennials'}], [{'sequence': '<s>Where do I live?</s>', 'score': 0.6903642416000366, 'token': 109, 'token_str': 'Ġdo'}, {'sequence': '<s>Where should I live?</s>', 'score': 0.15854182839393616, 'token': 197, 'token_str': 'Ġshould'}, {'sequence': '<s>Where did I live?</s>', 'score': 0.04364638775587082, 'token': 222, 'token_str': 'Ġdid'}, {'sequence': '<s>Where am I live?</s>', 'score': 0.030600957572460175, 'token': 524, 'token_str': 'Ġam'}, {'sequence': '<s>Where shall I live?</s>', 'score': 0.029068272560834885, 'token': 5658, 'token_str': 'Ġshall'}]]
```

It wouldn't be opposed to that design to return an array of values when there are several masks in the pipeline.

   "tokens" : ["the token ID used in filling MASK 1 ", "the token ID used in filling MASK 2", ... ],

```

body:
This will rank ('apple', 'France') and ('Paris', 'pie') higher than ('Paris', 'France'). We need some measure how happy the transformer is with each candidate sequence. I think we need additional forward passes to measure the effect of each combination. If there is some way of measuring the model's happiness with a candidate sequence one pass per candidate sequence will suffice. If not, I'd suggest to run
```
This apple is to <mask> what rice is to sushi.
This rhubarb is to <mask> what rice is to sushi.
This Paris is to <mask> what rice is to sushi.
This <mask> is to pie what rice is to sushi.
This <mask> is to France what rice is to sushi.
This <mask> is to biking what rice is to sushi.
```
and then multiple the probabilities. We will need some kind of beam search to limit the combinations tested as the number of forward passes needed will otherwise explode for more masked tokens or large `top_k`.

Edit: Actually, depending on the setting, this may run with fewer passes than trying all combinations, e.g. here 6 vs. 9.

Okey, I've been discussing quite a bit @patil-suraj about this. 
I do think that the functionality of the class will always be the same so it doesn't need to be Wav2Vec2 specific.
On the other hand, the docstring and the type checking is definitely very much different for each class.

I think there are three options:

a) Have only a single `Preprocessor` class that handles everything and only use this class for all models. The huge downside to me here is that it won't really be possible to have nice docstrings (linking to the correct feature extractor, tokenizer), and the type checking is not really possible. Also it's not really in line IMO with the general lib philosophy of having one level of abstraction model customized classes that inherit from a `Pretrained...` class. I guess `EncoderDecoderModel` is an exception, but it's definitely a downside for `EncoderDecoderModel` to me. Also there might be specific functionality that is different for some models, that we don't see yet.

b) Also make some kind of `PretrainedProcessor` that holds most of the functionality (even though there really isn't much) and overwrite the docstrings & type checking. For this we would still give the name `Wav2Vec2Processor`.

c) Leave it as it is.

=> taking this all into account I tend to b) & c) and since it's the first model of it's kind I'd just go for c) and leave it as it is now because we could always refactor it to b) without breaking change. I'm not really in favor of a) because of the reasons above, but maybe there is a huge advantage to a) I'm not seeing...What do you think @LysandreJik @sgugger ?

I don't think we need to add a new class for this as it's just a `ForSequenceClassification` with a different loss function.

I think this can all be done inside the regular `ForSequenceClassification` architecture by adding a flag defaulting to None and that can contain `"regression"`, `"single_label"` and `"multi_label"`. During the forward, if the flag is None, we try to find the best loss function (a bit like it's done right now while adding the BCE loss when the labels have 2 dims) and set the value of the flag, if the flag is set, we respect its value and apply the appropriate loss function.

This way when the model is saved, we can adapt the pipeline to take the flag into account and apply the right last layer (if the flag is there).
This also makes everything work properly with `Trainer`.

body:
Thanks for offering a PR and offering to clean things up! Unfortunately, I think here we're removing some functionality available to the user by obfuscating what was very visible before. It is now as simple as before to handle TPU trainings using `Trainer`, but is not so when using a custom training loop. 

Users would either have to rely on a private argument to specify their saving function, or rely on saving the state dict themselves, which is something that we do not recommend and something that has been shown to be incompatible even across minor versions.

While the previous version might have been hacky, I would argue it made for a simpler API for the user. I think we can work with what is proposed here too as it's definitely cleaner, but I'd like to keep simplicity of use at the center. What do you think?

body:
I'm not opposed to have this method! I think it could be made a bit better, for example with TF support. 

Also, wouldn't it be simpler to slightly change it so that it is a deep `torch.allclose`? We're used to having `torch.allclose` across the library, and we have some intuition of what `atol` or `rtol` we want. I think it would both stay closer to other tests, and make your testing code simpler, to have such a method.

I.e., instead of 

```py
self.assertEqual(
            deep_round(inputs),
            {
                # en_XX, A, test, EOS
                "input_ids": [[128022, 58, 4183, 2]],
                "attention_mask": [[1, 1, 1, 1]],
                # ar_AR
                "forced_bos_token_id": 44,
            },
        )
```

you would have

```py
self.assertTrue(
            deep_allclose(inputs, {
                # en_XX, A, test, EOS
                "input_ids": [[128022, 58, 4183, 2]],
                "attention_mask": [[1, 1, 1, 1]],
                # ar_AR
                "forced_bos_token_id": 44,
            }, atol=xxx, rtol=xxx)
        )
```

I don't feel strongly though, your current method (given TF support) is good already.
author: LysandreJik

body:
The biggest difference between your version and my version is understanding the `diff` when there is a mismatch.

If input_ids is changed, but the rest of the entries are equal, then usually the unittest output is very readable.

assertTrue on the other hand is a pretty nasty "False is not true" message, which doesn't really help (and for larger structures it's sometimes hard to pinpoint where the difference happened.

Your solution is what I was referring to when mentionning the `assertAlmostEqual` option (where I think we need to fuse `assertTrue` and `deep_allclose` to get consistent error messages, yet be able to keep allclose like comparisons.

For this PR, I'll stick to just add TF support for `deep_round` as its much simpler and keeps readable diffs.

body:
I only have a comment about:

> If there are assignees on the issue/PR, then it puts the following comment: f"This issue has been stale for a while, ping @{assignee.login}"

This creates unnecessary noise. e.g. one Issue that had 2 assignees received this comment twice for each assignee and we were notified twice as well on our own and each other's warning.

What I'm proposing is:
1. there should be only one comment issued regardless of how many assignees are 
2. 2a. To solve (1) easier I am not sure there is a need to mention the assignee at all - i.e. no need to make a special case for Issues with assignees - whatever the general message is sent is good enough. The assignee gets it anyway - I don't think an assignee can unsubscribe (I could be wrong), so the tagging doesn't add anything since the person is already subscribed.
   2b. if 2a doesn't resonate - well just tag both in the same comment ;)

Bottom line - if the subscribed person with the right perms wants to do something about the Issue/PR they can. If they don't tagging won't do anything useful OMHO.

Hey @elgeish,

Thanks a lot for your PR! Sorry that I only reviewed it now. In general I like the changes you have made to `run_wav2vec2.py` :-) 

A couple of things, I'd like to change:
- Remove the change from `modeling_wav2vec2.py`. I don't really want a resize lm head method in the model there -> it's too much of an edge case IMO. You can simply first instantiate the processor then use the tokenizer length to load the model with `Wav2Vec2ForCTC.from_pretrained(model_path, vocab_size=len(tokenizer))`. This way we don't need a `resize_lm_head()` method.
- Can you give me more context on the `buckwalter.json` file? 
- Can you also add more text to the README.md that explains a bit how to use the `run_wav2vec2.py` script? E.g. what does the orthography class do, what is the buckwalter vocab?
author: patrickvonplaten

body:
Yep, can you suggest a different way to increase the size of the linear layer's output to match bigger vocabs (e.g., for Arabic, it's 56)? I can move this method to `run_asr.py` or follow another approach.
I don't think it's about fine-tuning twice; it's about increasing the size of this layer's output:
https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/blob/c83fbc5f2d4355a13be52b086fe548f3c43e8ec8/src/transformers/models/wav2vec2/modeling_wav2vec2.py#L978

author: elgeish

body:
Gottcha, yeah in this case, I don't think we need any resizing method at all! What I'd suggest is to do the following. 
1. First instantiate the tokenizer with the vocab as you wish. The correct vocab size is then defined by `len(tokenizer)`.
2. Second, load the model. Now you can load the model as follows: `model = Wav2Vec2ForCTC.from_pretrained("facebook/wav2vec2-base", vocab_size=len(tokenizer))`. The model should then have the correct lm head size. 

Also note that all "pretrained-only" checkpoints don't have any weights for the `lm_head` you can see this when *e.g.* loading the model: ```Wav2Vec2ForCTC.from_pretrained("facebook/wav2vec2-base")``` should show a warning that says that the lm head was randomly initialized because those weights aren't stored in the checkpoint. I tried to explain this in the blog as well: https://huggingface.co/blog/fine-tune-xlsr-wav2vec2

I admit it's a little bit hacky because the encoder won't be run and hence the `input_ids` won't be used; the `input_ids` is created just to satisfy the subsequent processing, which depends on it for the input shape. The value -100 is chosen so that if the `input_ids` were accidentally used for actual encoding, an error would be thrown.

I notice there is a relatively new argument `encoder_no_repeat_ngram_size`, which would make the logits processor dependent on the encoder input_ids. Because the dummy input_ids would be all -100, which is impossible for `decoder_input_ids`, this won't have any unexpected effect.

body:
The problem is that it leads to:
1. To multiple points of language pair definition which leads to error-prone execution when those go out of sync (user modified one of them but not the other). The language pair should be specified once
2. The software shouldn't subtly misbehave if some flag is passed or not. At the very least the example script should require `--source_prefix` cl arg if the model is of type `*t5*` - it must not be optional.

Combining these 2 together is what @theo-m  implemented.

I'm voting against this. 3 reasons from my side:

- This is not in line with "simple notebooks" that are easy to tweak. I think we somewhat decided that notebooks should not follow the one-size-fits-it-all approach.
- We add those lines only for 5 checkpoints, while we could very well just let the user define the prefix. A user that knows how T5 was trained can insert the prefix. Also, for a user that doesn't know T5 this happens automatically which could mean that she/he might not be aware afterward that a prefix has to be added to make summarization work.
- People that fine-tune a model like `t5-large` don't necessarily need the summarization prefix to work. `t5-large` can very well be fine-tuned without a prefix (not the strongest argument).

I don't think we can do this change at all tbh. This is very backward's breaking and would mean that the beam search generation of everybody is affected.

I agree that the next_token_scores are not normalized anymore after having applied `logits_processor`, but it's not something we can change really anymore IMO since so many models rely on `beam_search`.

One thing we could do though to help your use case would maybe to add a new optional "Normalizer" `logits_processor` that would normalize the output after all other logits processors have been applied. Would that maybe help solve your use case?

I understand this would break everybody's code, but the actual implementation of beam search is flawed. It's not just my use case but everybody's.

What if we add a flag to `generate` like `add_beam_search_normalization_fix` that optionally re-normalizes the scores after the logits processors? And then, when introducing more breaking changes (a major version change?), make it the default?

The reason I coded this as an 2nd loop is to:

1. minimize the overhead - why calculate many things if we aren't using them, so to run just the bare minimum of code. There are 5 of these, and some of them run a lot more code than greedy_search.
2. to avoid complicating the existing code by separating the special needs into its own separate if branch so it's very easy to tell when studying the coder or running a debugger that this is a separate things I don't need to worry about
3. we must ensure that all forward calls will be repeated, I just wasn't sure if some model decides to take a shortcut if we feed it an input that it deems unnecessary to run forward with, so as a caution I was replaying that exact last input input that produced a full forward run. It's possible that no model has the smarts to do any internal shortcutting and my worry was unnecessary.

If you feel that solving this within the existing while loop is a better solution I will adapt to it.

while sync.item() > 0.0:

    sync =torch.tensor(0.0 if am_i_done() else 1.0)
    torch.distributed.allreduce(sync)
```

There are 5 different versions of search functions and what I did is to bring them in sync on the order of how the last 4-5 chunks of code is done. e.g. `cur_len` was incremented inconsistently in several places - the only reason it wasn't breaking things is that the functions called using `cur_len` weren't impacting the outcome outside the loop. But it could.

````

body:
See latest version for my proposal:
- `extra-quality-checks` common processes for quality and fixup, checks that are fast or need to run on all files, not changing any file
- `extra-style-checks` common processes for style and fixup, checks that are fast or need to run on all files, changing files if necessary
- `style` style all files + other checks that are "writing" the right thing
- `quality` check all files + other checks (in check only mode)
-  `fixup` same as `style` + `quality` but only on modified files.

body:
It doesn't throw because if one doesn't have any version of TensorFlow installed, we never enter the 
```py
    if _tf_available:
```
statement at line 86!

This would crash if we were to install another version of TensorFlow that is not in the list of candidates: `_tf_available` would be `True` as the spec for `tensorflow` would be found, but no `_tf_version` would be set as the exact package wouldn't be found. 

An example of such a package that comes to mind is the TensorFlow fork for M1 macs: https://github.com/apple/tensorflow_macos
author: LysandreJik

This is a tremendous improvement relative to the previous implementation, great job @stas00!

The only thing I'm wondering about is the addition of `psutils` to the core dependencies. Having a hard requirement on it seems unnecessary. Would a soft dependency with a warning when not installed work for you? Happy to discuss if you think otherwise.
author: LysandreJik

body:
Usually not too keen on adding a new dependency to the core dependencies. Staying slim is a good way to prevent conflicts and to not break everything when there is an issue with another library; so we usually prefer adding soft dependencies to hard dependencies.

Is there something here that would prevent adding `psutil` as a soft dependency, rather than a hard one?

This case seems pretty narrow, as users that don't use the trainer (e.g., only use it for inference, or training with their custom loop/other libraries, only use pipelines, etc) don't need to have that in their system. 

This is how the hard dependencies are defined, with historical exceptions for regex and sacremoses, which could eventually be removed from the hard dependencies. Sacremoses is here because it's necessary to use for the XLM tokenizer, which, unfortunately, will never have a fast tokenizer.

body:
While it seems to be very bad practice to adapt an existing tokenizer file to add a new model, I strongly advocate to do so here. The reasons are the following:

- The official tokenizer is a pegasus tokenizer, see [here](https://github.com/google-research/bigbird/blob/master/bigbird/vocab/pegasus.model).
- The previous implementation was very restrictive by forcing `offset` to be of a certain value, which is too specific for a general PEGASUS like model IMO
- The required adaptions to the existing tokenizer file are ok IMO: We add the possibility of the `mask_sent_token` to be `None` & allow `offsets` to be whatever value fits.

I'm actually not sure whether using MBart's way of creating the `decoder_input_ids` here is correct. Note that MBart uses a very special language-dependent pattern when fine-tuning so that the `decoder_start_token_id` depends on the language, see Fig. 1 of [paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2001.08210.pdf). 

IMO, this is not the case for FSMT. FSMT always uses the EOS/SEP token as the `decoder_start_token_id = sep_token_id = "<\s>"` if I understand correctly => Think it's better therefore to copy the `shift_tokens_right` function from Bart and set `decoder_start_token_id = 2` as a default in the config. This looks great. The tokenizer code is complex but you've managed to make it clear so that the review (which should also apply if a user reads the code) was simple.

Thank you for adding a nice battery of tests as well.

For @sgugger as we discussed this might be an issue initially:

I guess the first thing that comes to mind when reading this PR is whether all the logic regarding entities should be separated from the tokenizer (i.e, in a pre-processing script in examples), or stay in the tokenizer. I feel that the current implementation is a good choice because:

- LUKE seems to have been designed around entities and should always be used with them
- IDs, attention masks, position IDs, and token type IDs like traditional tokenizers, but for entities additionally
- Makes it way simpler to use as-is rather than having all of that in a separate script.

Additionally, a thought that might occur is whether we'd prefer that in a feature processor, but I think this is better suited for the tokenizer as well, as it is entirely text-based and akin to other features the existing tokenizers possess.

I appreciate the intent of this PR, but I think it's most likely to hit users in their own foot without them even realizing. I'm disapproving this PR for that reason (and it actually raises questions about other pipelines implementations)

- Pipelines are aimed at inference, and in inference, batching is almost always detrimental. I've modified the proposed example with a slightly less nice example to display the problem:
https://gist.github.com/Narsil/ee5c09875e74fa6f018dc6d014f6c06c. 
```
Model batch size 1  
Device: CPU (i7-4790)
No. examples: 200
Time taken: 10.693870067596436
Model batch size 2
Device: CPU (batched)
No. examples: 200
Time taken: 10.754503965377808
Model batch size 2
Device: CPU (batched 2nd)
No. examples: 200
Time taken: 34.8472113609314
-------------------------------------------------- (GTX 970)
Model batch size 1
Device: GPU
No. examples: 200
Time taken: 0.7129480838775635
Model batch size 2
Device: GPU (batched)
No. examples: 200
Time taken: 0.708709716796875
Model batch size 2
Device: GPU (batched 2nd)
No. examples: 200
Time taken: 8.97895359992981

```
The core of the issue is the extra padding tokens created while running inference. Those are very bad for overall efficiency, and in a live system it is most likely to occur (from experience, I can say that it can be overwhelmingly bad). It's almost never worth it to attempt batching in a live production, unless you're very sure about the alignment problem.
- That being noted, other pipelines do sometimes do batching, and it **can** be effective if used properly, even if it is very hard at the pipeline level (because we're receiving strings and not TOKENS, which should be used for nice alignment)

body:
The `temp` stands for `temperature`, I've updated the names to be more descriptive now, and added docstrings for them (see `gumbel_softmax_temperature`)
The values are `(max temp, min temp, annealing factor)` 
The temperature starts at the max value (2.0) and can be annealed at every batch update by a given factor
using a custom callback:
```python
class GumbelTempCallback(TrainerCallback):
    def on_step_begin(self, args, state, control, model: Wav2Vec2ForPreTraining, **kwargs):
        model.update_gumbel_temperature(state.global_step)

trainer = Trainer(...)
trainer.add_callback(GumbelTempCallback)
```

-------
`logit_temp` is now `contrastive_logit_temperature`, or `\kappa` in the contrastive loss:

body:
`librosa` is not a dependency currently, I'm more than hesitant to add it for just that feature.

Also `librosa` api enforces to use a filename which is pretty bad in the context of an API (where hitting disk is never desirable). It does fallback to ffmpeg anyway, in pretty much what `ffmpeg_read` does. (Actually if you use soundfile and resample later then you're also wasting a lot of time, it's much better if the file can be read at the correct sampling rate directly).

The main issue I think is : should we have such functions in `transformers` ? 
It makes life easier on users which is Priority number 1 of the lib (especially pipelines).
At the same time, I don't think we want to reinvent all image/audio preprocessing.

Note: `torchaudio` is another alternative to `librosa` to consider too. (it doesn't do automatic resampling afaik)
author: Narsil

body: @mpariente and @jonashaag might also want to chime in on this because I remember having discussions on this subject with them
author: julien-c

body:
The question is what is your priority.

- If you are looking to minimise dependencies while being able to read a lot of file types, this way is probably best. (Could switch the manual ffmpeg invocation for the `audioread` library.)
- If you are looking to minimise load time, then trying soundfile + [julius](https://github.com/adefossez/julius) is probably the best choice. (Could also add a fallback to ffmpeg.)
- To keep things as simple as possible and to write as little code as possible, just use `librosa.load` which tries soundfile first and then falls back to ffmpeg.

> (Actually if you use soundfile and resample later then you're also wasting a lot of time, it's much better if the file can be read at the correct sampling rate directly).

I don't think this is correct since ffmpeg also needs to do resampling, so it depends on the speed of ffmpeg resampling implementation vs. your resampling implementation.

body:
Ok, I think this could be the way to go for weight sharing - it's different from the PyTorch design where the weights are shared before the forward pass & therefore there is less code duplication in PyTorch as we can have a general function for it. 

If I understood correctly this is more difficult in Flax, so I think this is a good solution for now. It will mean that we'll re-write this code in all models that have weight sharing, but on the bright side it's also arguably less "magic" and the user has an easier time understanding that weights are shared when tracing a forward pass.

=> What do you think @sgugger @CoderPat @avital @marcvanzee ?
author: patrickvonplaten

body: Yeah, I took this approach from the solution proposed [here](https://github.com/google/flax/discussions/1264#discussioncomment-644887). The problem mostly is that we are quite restricted by the modularization structure to match PyTorch's ones. I think for your approach to work, we would have to create the layer outside of the word embedding module which doesn't work well with PyTorch's weight structure

Actually, Electra doesn't tie the word embeddings at all, so I don't think we need the logic here :-)

To give a bit more detail here:

In PyTorch, we call the function [_tie_or_clone_weights()](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/blob/04ab2ca639ee6fd1002ce0a498d892245f0c9093/src/transformers/modeling_utils.py#L581) on every model class that:
- has `self.config.tie_word_embeddings` set to True (this is the case for ELECTRA)
- **and** that overwrites the function `get_output_embeddings()` to return output embeddings != None (this is **not** the case for ELECTRA)

=> no weights are tied

body:
This won't work sadly, for two reasons.
1. First, everything in the `__dict__` of the config gets serialized when one uses `config.self_pretrained()` (which is called by `model.from_pretrained`) so any other model downloaded from the hub with a checkpoint saved after this is merged will get this attribute in the config. Then if a user instantiates a randomly-initialized model using the config, with the following code:
```python
config = AutoConfig.from_pretrained("new_checkpoint_after_this_is_merge")
model = AutoModel.from_config(config)
```
then the model won't be randomly initalized (at least not with `_init_weights`) since the config will have this `use_pretrained_weights`.

2. Then come the problem that pretrained model instantiated with `from_pretrained` does not necessarily have all weights initialized (if you discard the head to put another task-specific head) and this PR will break the way those weights are randomly initialized.

I sadly don't see a way around passing around a list of not-initialized weights from pretrained to the `_init_weights` function
author: sgugger

body:
- I'm not a huge fan of "attaching" a new parameter to the `config` which is not really understandable by the user.

- Also, I think this could lead to problems -> lots of people initialize all weights **except** the final layer weights from a pre-trained BERT in, *e.g.* a `BertForSequenceClassification`. The logic would then not correctly initialize the final layer, but simply set everything to zero which would probably lead to a worse fine-tuning of `BertForSequenceClassification`. 

=> I would propose the following:

1) When using `from_pretrained(...)`, we pass a new parameter to `model = cls(config, *model_args, **model_kwargs)` by setting `model_kwargs["init_weights"] = False`. This then sadly means that we have to replace all `__init__(self, config)` functions in the modeling files by `__init__(self, config, init_weights=True)`, but I think we can use a regex for this. This is a huge change in terms of files that need to be changed, but I think it's cleaner then creating a new `"use_pretrained_weights"` config parameter that the user shouldn't have to learn about. Then, we also need to change `self.init_weights()` with 

```python
if init_weights:
   self.init_weights()
```

2) Now, we also need to take care of cases where only parts of the model are initialized from pre-trained weights. The other part still needs to be initialized. Here we can't simply use `self.init_weights()` because it would necessarly run through all modules and initialized them. So I think we should leverage the `missing_keys()` list here to extract all `nn.Modules(...)` that still need to be initialized and then run `self._init_weights(m) for m in uninitialized_modules`

```

body:
The `init_weights` kwarg on its own won't work, but it's necessary to prevent each model from calling `self.init_weights()`. 

The order of operations when doing `BertModel.from_pretrained(...)` is the following:

1) Instantiate a random model: `cls(config, *model_args, **model_kwargs)` => this command already calls `self.init_weights(...)` (since in every model class we have a `self.init_weights(...)` in `__init__(config):. So in order to prevent this we need to pass a flag to `cls(config, *model_args, **model_kwargs)` which I would do with `model_kwargs["init_weights"] = False`.

2) Only after the model is instantiated (and the weights already have values), we can know which weights were missing & thus need to be randomely initialized. Here we can retrieve `uninitialized_weights`, but it would be better to actually retrieve all `nn.Modules` that are randomely initialized since then we can reuse each model's `_init_weights(...)` function.

3) Having retrieved `uninitialized_modules` we can run `self._init_weights(...)` on each module.

body:
Both implementations proposed overlook the weights of the base transformer model.

This is an issue as if some weights of the base transformer model are missing in the checkpoint file, they don't end up in the `unintialized_modules` returned by this method; they're not used with the `init_weight()` method.

See below for a reproducible code example. If one saves a torch state dict without the base model prefix and reloads it in a model that has the model prefix, then the two methods here are unable to identify the missing weights. Such a use-case is for dropping a model head, for example.

```py
from transformers import BertModel, BertForSequenceClassification, BertConfig
import torch

model = BertModel.from_pretrained("bert-base-uncased")
state_dict = model.state_dict()
del state_dict["embeddings.word_embeddings.weight"]

model.save_pretrained("save_it_here")
torch.save(state_dict, "save_it_here/pytorch_model.bin")

model = BertForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("save_it_here", initializer_range=0.00001)

print(model.bert.embeddings.word_embeddings.weight)
```

This crashes with the current implementation, and with @sgugger's proposal, the resulting embeddings have the following values on my machine (way above what they should be given the initializer range given above):
```
tensor([[ 0.0000,  0.0000,  0.0000,  ...,  0.0000,  0.0000,  0.0000],
        [ 0.5985,  0.1010,  0.0665,  ..., -0.6634, -0.4788, -0.5904],
        [ 3.4545,  0.4866,  0.8241,  ..., -1.4983, -0.4970, -1.3458],
```

on `master` I get the following output:

```
tensor([[ 0.0000e+00,  0.0000e+00,  0.0000e+00,  ...,  0.0000e+00,
          0.0000e+00,  0.0000e+00],
        [ 6.3332e-06,  5.1651e-07, -3.1017e-06,  ...,  4.8352e-07,
          1.2032e-05,  5.6933e-06],
```

This is a bit of a far-fetched use-case as I can't imagine when one would delete a value from the state dict this way, it's just to get an idea of something we're missing.
author: LysandreJik

Reviewed until feature extractor/modeling because I'm not sure you're finished. Let me know if that's the case and I'll review the rest.

Regarding your questions:

### panopticapi

How much of the panopticapi package is necessary? If it's only the `rgb2id` utility, then would it be possible to have it inside the library with the appropriate credits/copyright?

If the panopticapi package is used extensively for panoptic segmentation, then your first proposal (having  a `task` option to determine which packages should be available at runtime) sounds good to me, but happy to hear @sgugger, @patrickvonplaten and @patil-suraj's thoughts.

### The config attribute `return_intermediate_layers`

I'm not too keen on setting a config flag to a value manually within the model directly. I would rather this configuration value be used in a similar fashion as `output_hidden_states`: have the ability to override the configuration value when calling the `forward` method. This way the configuration property remains unchanged and the wrapping model (here `DetrForPanopticSegmentation`) can handle that configuration property as a standalone property.

I wonder if it should even be a configuration value if it should always have a certain value for some models? If some models require it to be set to `True` and some models require it to be set to `False`, what advantage is there to give the user the ability to change it? From the implementation it seems like an internal component that the user shouldn't concern themselves with.

### timm

It seems you've already added support for `is_timm_available()`, which is great. Cool to have it as an optional dependency!

@rwightman do you want to take a look at this implementation? This would add an optional dependency to `timm`, in return offering any `timm` model to be used as a backbone for DETR.

Completely agree with you here ! I am not a fan either, but it seemed like the simplest possible change currently.

However the 2 classes *are* quite different:
- Wav2vec2 does ASR in a single pass,
- S2T needs to run generate.
Hence this: https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/blob/master/src/transformers/pipelines/automatic_speech_recognition.py#L141

I really think there is no way to avoid it thinking about what `ForConditionalGeneration` and `ForCTC`  to fuse them in some sort of common `For` class. The heads are very different and should be used differently.
There are also differences in the tokenizers (in CTC, `pad` is used to split multiple letters, whereas you want to remove `pad`  in S2T).

We could also imagine having 2 different pipelines, but it feels clunky too because the 2 pipelines API are exactly the same.

Actually, the more I think about it, the more I'm tending towards creating two pipelines:

`automatic-speech-recognition-seq2seq` and `automatic-speech-recognition-ctc` with `...-seq2seq` supporting a `S2T` and `-ctc` supporting Wav2Vec2. Then we can have `S2T` in `AutoModelForConditionalGeneration` and create a `AutoModelForCTC` for Wav2Vec2. Think this would be the cleanest approach.

Another more hacky solution would be to just have `automatic-speech-recognition` with one `AutoModelForAutomaticSpeechRecognition` class. Wav2Vec2 can and probably will have multiple classes for ASR (CTC, Seq2Seq, CTC + LM) so to support this we would have to then add a tuple of possible Wav2vec2 classes for `AutoModelForAutomaticSpeechRecognition`, which IMO is not super cleann. Also, this would break consistency a bit since usually our `AutoModel....` classes correspond very much directly to the model class name `ForSequenceClassification` => `BertForSequenceClassification`. 

So, I'm tending towards splitting the pipeline and deprecating `automatic-speech-recognition` - what do you think @Narsil ?

(Sorry, I should have probably made a better review when you added `automatic-speech-recognition`)

body:
I think in Flax the user should never pass `use_cache` but should handle everything over:

1) `init_cache(...)` and 
2) passing `past_key_values` or not

It's not possible to pass `use_cache` in the first pass to retrieve the `past_key_values` like we do it in PyTorch, but we need to call `init_cache(...)` first to get 0 padded `past_key_values` => I think it's better to handle everything over `past_key_values` afterward instead of making `use_cache` public method that would always have to be `True` when `past_key_values` is passed and always be `False` when `past_key_values=None`.

We still need to pass down the boolean though so that `init_cache(...)` can tell `FlaxGPT2Attention` to initialize the cache. 

=> Another option would be to instead of passing along `_use_cache`, we set a config parameter of `FlaxGPT2Attention` called `is_decoder` to `True` when `past_key_values` and to `False` when it is not instead of passing down a boolean flag & then have no `use_cache` at all? Is this maybe better? @sgugger
author: patrickvonplaten

In distributed training, the torch generator should have the same state on all processes since it's set with the same seed initially (then all processes execute the same code). Unless someone goes out of their way to only execute a random instruction on one process.

body:
I am not sure my comment communicated the problem well:

- Under NLP models you get inputs of `int64` and they get converted to the correct variation of `float` via the embedding - so we get fp32 if the model is normal, or fp16 if it's `model.half()` 
- wav2vec2 inputs are `float32` - and they don't have an embedding to auto-convert them to the right dtype. How could deepspeed possibly guess what user's inputs are supposed to be? It's the Trainer that needs to set `inputs.to(dtype)`. e.g. how could it know what to do with inputs of `int64`
- AMP doesn't change the dtype of user inputs, since it never works with fp16 directly unless the user set the inputs to it and only adjusts things dynamically to fp16 during some of the computations. 

If you have an idea of how this deriving can be automated, I'm all ears. I'm just not sure how Deepspeed could possibly know what user has in mind.

Do you perhaps propose that if the inputs are fp32 then Deepspeed can automatically convert them to fp16 if it's doing its amp version? But if inputs are anything else than fp32 (e.g. int64`) it should leave them alone?
author: stas00

author: stas00

body:
> - AMP doesn't change the dtype of user inputs, since it never works with fp16 directly unless the user set the inputs to it and only adjusts things dynamically to fp16 during some of the computations.

That is incorrect. Inside the autocast context manager, the conversion is done automatically, so the user does not have to think about the dtype of the inputs. In the [official AMP tutorial](https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/notes/amp_examples.html#typical-mixed-precision-training) there is no inputs dtype conversion and having int inputs is a specificity of NLP, not the general rule. All CV models have float inputs and I think that is still the majority of Deep Learning models.

DeepSpeed could also properly deal with dtype of the inputs since they wrap the model in their own container. I'm just noticing a point where they could make their API better and more aligned with PyTorch, I have no problem with merging this like I said before.
author: sgugger

Yes, yes, I'm not arguing, just trying to understand how they could do it in a safe way. We may merge this to move wav2vec2 along and meanwhile I'm talking to Deepspeed about automating this and once it's there to drop my workaround.

I stepped through https://pytorch.org/tutorials/recipes/recipes/amp_recipe.html  in debugger and it doesn't convert inputs to fp16 in mixed precision, it sends inputs to Linear in fp32 and converts them on the fly to fp16, returning fp16 result.

That's said: over at Deepspeed we are discussing automatically converting fp32 to fp16 under fp16 enabled and having a special flag to prevent that from happening should someone not want that behavior.

@LysandreJik @sgugger   RoFormerTokenizer is not identical to BertTokenizer when tokenizing Chinese chars. 
So we need to create a new file for RoFormerTokenizer.

```python
import jieba
from transformers import BertTokenizer,RoFormerTokenizer

jieba.lcut(zh_text,HMM=False)
# ['今天天气', '非常', '好', '！']

# difference
bert_tokenzier = BertTokenizer.from_pretrained("junnyu/roformer_chinese_base")
roformer_tokenizer = RoFormerTokenizer.from_pretrained("junnyu/roformer_chinese_base")
zh_text = "今天天气非常好！"
bert_output = bert_tokenzier.tokenize(zh_text)
roformer_output = roformer_tokenizer.tokenize(zh_text)
print(bert_output) 
print(roformer_output) 
# ['今', '天', '天', '气', '非', '常', '好', '！']
# ['今', '天', '天', '气', '非常', '好', '！']

# same
en_text = "I love Beijing, Beijing is the capital of China!"
bert_output = bert_tokenzier.tokenize(en_text)
roformer_output = roformer_tokenizer.tokenize(en_text)
 # ['i', 'love', 'be', '##i', '##jing', ',', 'be', '##i', '##jing', 'is', 'the', 'capital', 'of', 'china', '!']
 # ['i', 'love', 'be', '##i', '##jing', ',', 'be', '##i', '##jing', 'is', 'the', 'capital', 'of', 'china', '!']
print(bert_output)
print(roformer_output)

```
In this case, `今天天气` and `非常`  are meaningful words. We shouldn't split them into single char. 
For  `今天天气`, this word do not exist in the vocabulary，we should use original BertTokenizer to tokenize them. 
we got `今 ` 、`天`、 `天`、 `气`.
For `非常` , this word do exist in the vocabulary, we do not use original BertTokenizer to tokenize them.

My biggest concern here are the position_ids since they are quite often absolute. 
E.g. in GPT2, every input_id from position 0 to 1024 get a unique id, which is then cached, so when the 1025 tokens comes, the tokens 1024, 1025 will have the same position id, just like all other tokens coming after the 1024th one => this is problematic IMO. What I mean to say is, in flax we init the model by doing a forward pass so we need to pass an example, which is created using this `input_shape`. Here the `num_patches` depend on the `image_size` and `patch_size`, and `num_patches` is used to init the embedding layer. 

The default `input_shape` is the shape used by pre-trained model which would be (224, 224, 3) but in our tests, we use different `image_size` but we don't pass `input_shape` in tests, so in this case, it results in in-correct `num_patches` and there is shape mismatch when adding the embeddings because `input_shape` and current `image_size` in the test are different.

Maybe we should pass `input_shape` when initing the model in tests.

In Flax, 2D Conv layer expects `kernel_size` and `stride` to be tuple, also to be compatible with pytorch's conv 
we need to use `VALID` padding. So this should look like

```python
nn.Conv(
        embed_dim,
        kernel_size=(patch_size, patch_size),
        strides=(patch_size, patch_size),
        padding="VALID",
        dtype=self.dtype,
        kernel_init=jax.nn.initializers.normal(),
)
```

You shouldn't need to add space for special symbols because the special IDs are defined to be codepoints in the Private Use Area, as seen in lines 34-38 above, which are still valid codepoints (they just happen to be codepoints that will never be assigned to characters), and are therefore within the full Unicode codespace.

body: This doesn't seem right to me. Ideally the model would always run directly on the codepoints of the string, so it should never have to deal with something whose string form does not have lenth == 1. That's why we define those special codepoints (lines 34-38 above). In other words, I would expect this to be `chr(CLS)` (i.e, `chr(0xE000)`).  The benefit of doing it that way is that the only preprocess you ever have to do is just `[ord(c) for c in input_string]`. If you define the special symbols with multi-character strings, then you actually have to parse through the string to look for them and handle them.

from transformers import CanineTokenizer, CanineModel

model_inputs = tokenizer(["Life is like a box of chocolates.", "Today is Monday."], padding="longest", return_tensors="pt")

outputs = model(**model_inputs) # forward pass

```python

# hidden states at this point are:
#tensor([[[-0.3558, -0.3452, -0.4650,  ...,  0.1620,  0.0945,  0.0383],                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       
#         [-0.3339,  0.0142, -0.0850,  ..., -0.1798, -0.3543,  0.1104],                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        
#         [-0.0886,  0.1268, -0.1317,  ..., -0.1621,  0.0503, -0.0632],                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        
#         ...,                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 
#         [-0.2179, -0.1023, -0.0681,  ..., -0.1923, -0.3228,  0.0826],                               
#         [-0.0679, -0.1213, -0.0621,  ..., -0.2119, -0.2003,  0.1054],     
#         [-0.0779,  0.2627, -0.0289,  ..., -0.0358, -0.0487,  0.0313]]],            
#       grad_fn=<AddBackward0>)  

for i, layer_module in enumerate(self.layer):
    if output_hidden_states:
        all_hidden_states = all_hidden_states + (hidden_states,)

    layer_head_mask = head_mask[i] if head_mask is not None else None
    past_key_value = past_key_values[i] if past_key_values is not None else None

    if getattr(self.config, "gradient_checkpointing", False) and self.training:

        if use_cache:
            logger.warning(
                "`use_cache=True` is incompatible with `config.gradient_checkpointing=True`. Setting "
                "`use_cache=False`..."
            )
            use_cache = False

        def create_custom_forward(module):
            def custom_forward(*inputs):
                return module(*inputs, past_key_value, output_attentions)

            return custom_forward

        layer_outputs = torch.utils.checkpoint.checkpoint(
            create_custom_forward(layer_module),

Code here tries to mimic the `normalize_before` logic from `fairseq`:

https://github.com/pytorch/fairseq/blob/4950c56f461db1646872159b2c470fe57ae72c69/fairseq/modules/transformer_layer.py#L132-L145

```python
if self.normalize_before:
    x = self.self_attn_layer_norm(x)
x, _ = self.self_attn(
    query=x,
    key=x,
    value=x,
    key_padding_mask=encoder_padding_mask,
    need_weights=False,
    attn_mask=attn_mask,
)
x = self.dropout_module(x)
x = self.residual_connection(x, residual)
if not self.normalize_before:
    x = self.self_attn_layer_norm(x)
```

body:
The way local attention was implemented caused very high VRAM use with certain, especially prime, sequence lengths as described in #11320:

![patched](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/82650881/115746923-0ee0cc00-a395-11eb-9bcd-c289a38c77b5.png)

The green line is the original implementation's VRAM use in GB over sequence length. Padding inputs to multiples of the local attention window sizes mitigates this, but the code is still hard to follow. The way local attention is implemented in this PR follows PR #11630. Instead of the very complex folding approach, it is calculated like global attention with an adjusted mask, which masks out attention values beyond the local attention window. This is much simpler, easier to understand and does not seem to have any noticable negative performance impact. It also fixes the issue with high VRAM usage.

Is there any way to get reliably a vocab (or reverse vocab) ? That undermines the purpose of this PR which is to add fast lookup. `get_vocab()` exists and is mandatory for all fast tokenizers for instance.

In this case we don't really need to `tokenize` but really just a way to get corresponding ids to reduce the potential targets.
The rationale here is:
- Fast lookup
- If lookup fail, slow tokenization and take first token. It will enable more "natural" usage but still most likely slightly wrong.

If "something" does not correspond to a single token ("some", + "thing") but is in the target list, then we will filter on "some" and it will be a possible output of the fill-mask which is .. subpar but best effort.

This stuff is T5-specific only. In that case, during decoding when:
- `encoder_outputs` are fed into the model solely without `encoder_attentions` and `encoder_hidden_states`, and
- `output_attentions=True` or `output_hidden_states=True`,

the error occurs in this part of code.

```
elif isinstance(inputs["encoder_outputs"], tuple):
    last_hidden_state = inputs["encoder_outputs"][0]
    hidden_states = None
    attentions = None
    idx = 0
    if inputs["output_hidden_states"]:
        idx += 1
        hidden_states = inputs["encoder_outputs"][idx]
    if inputs["output_attentions"]:
        idx += 1
        attentions = inputs["encoder_outputs"][idx]

    inputs["encoder_outputs"] = TFBaseModelOutput(
        last_hidden_state=last_hidden_state,
        hidden_states=hidden_states,
        attentions=attentions,
    )
```
This results from that neither `output_attentions` nor `output_hidden_states` is present in the inputs["output_hidden_states"] because encoder pass is done if and only if -- `if inputs["encoder_outputs"] is None`.

You can pass multiple elements to that, which will be broadcasted. So if you have e.g. 3 special tokens, then you'll get an extra dimension of length 3 in the output, and you can just squash that with `tf.math.reduce_any()` to see if any of the special tokens matched, without needing a cast to `tf.int32`.

body:
That's an option that is definitely viable.

The core things I think are important:

- If a user specified something, we need to respect it
- If something comes as a default it cannot override anything user specified.
- If user specification are unclear/unsound, yell loud and clear about what is going on, and what the code is going to do to save the `generate`.

Option 1 (current):
```python
model.generate(...., no_repeat_n_tokens=3)
```
I need to add some even more clever functionality
```python
mylogitsProcessor=LogitsProcessorList(MyLogits())
model.generate(...., logits_processor=mylogitsProcessor, no_repeat_n_tokens=3)
```
(You can keep the easiness of `generate`).

Option 2 (logits_processor is a full override):
```python
model.generate(..., no_repeat_n_tokens=3)
```
becomes
```python
my_logits_processor = LogitsProcessorList(
   NoRepeatLogitsProcessor(3),
  MyLogits()
)
model.generate(..., logits_processor=logits_processor)
```

Option 1 has the advantage that we can keep some options simpler to use and still add some custom logits processor, if we're careful enough that no non-user defined variable can ever override the `logits_processor` in a hidden way, then we're good to go. (Only user defined arguments are able to modify). This is ofc a guarantee that might be tricky to keep in the future, so we are taking a risk of silently breaking things. It also makes user code trickier to understand since there is no ONE way to define logits_processor, so it might lead to hard to understand behavior.


Option 2 has the advantage that it has a single point of definition of logits processor. The disadvantage is that it requires more changes on the user the first time he uses this variable. We also need to yell quite strongly that we're simply ignoring every other argument, which might not be obvious (we could even crash at this point, since it's a really easy to overlook thing and will definitely yield poor results). 

IMHO, both are really fine, we just need to stick to one option. I suggested to @lvwerra Option 1, because I thought that `max_length` was the only variable that was always defined even if not user supplied. If this assumption is wrong and hard to make on a small list of variable, then I don't think we should stick with Option 1. Option 2 does have drawbacks as we're rejecting complexity back into user code instead of absorbing it like we're doing right now. But it does help separation of concern.

body:
That's a good argument @lvwerra and I fully understand what you mean. 

I'm however really concerned about the complexity that option 1 adds for IMO very few use cases. Also from a backwards breaking point of view it's pretty much impossible to go from option 1 to option 2 in the future if this feature becomes more important where as it's much easier to go from option 2 to option 1 in the future.

> For me the main use-case is to add a custom processer/criteria in addition to what I can already do with the kwargs. Otherwise, why go the extra step of using the arguably more complicated API if you can just pass it as an argument.

Very good point and that's the big drawback of option 2. I believe that people having to use special logits processors are able to create it themselves. 

Ok, how about we do something in between option 1 and option 2 that doesn't create a crazy complex logic. 

If one passes a logits processor, we do the following:
1) just create the normal logits_processor that would have been created without passing one.
2) if any object of the passed logits processor is in the already created logits processor then we raise an error and tell the user which logits processor was created twice (and ideally which paramter has to be changed for this)
3) If there is no error make a union of the two lists and we're good to go.

body:
IMO Flax is definitely different from PyTorch in a sense that it is not enough to just import the model and tokenizer for training. Given that in Flax the gradients are computed by calling `jax.grad` on the loss function, we just cannot have the same API as in PyTorch. 

Given that , the training script should be responsible for everything training related and not the model. So I do prefer to not attach `shift_tokens_right` to the model. 

Regarding the solution proposed above: Yes the user will have to import a non-public method `shift_tokens_right` from the model, but I don't see a problem with that. 

Another solution would actually be to just not important the method and rewrite it in the training script. As far as I remember it's only MBart that uses a different `shift_tokens_right` method. 

What do you think?

Isn't this a bug? Why do we want fp16 models loaded as fp32? That was the whole point of this PR - to not do that.

Pytorch doesn't have all ops implemented on CPU for Half. But I don't think we should automatically compensate for that, since it'd prevent situations where it works just fine. If the model.half doesn't work under CPU it's not a bug, but a pytorch limitation. Users can request the missing on Half features to be implemented.

Users can switch the model to fp32 if they need to.

so basically we were hiding the limitation all along and now when the library does the right thing, the limitation has become visible. But this is not a transformers issue.

> So we should actually leave the model as it was for a good test of that!

You meant, leaving the breaking test as is, rather than working around it - and finding a fix instead.

Then I would rather make a special test which tests this thing, otherwise this test caught the problem absolutely accidentally.

body:
> Why do we want fp16 models loaded as fp32?

Because FP16 does not work on CPU and if all the models saved in FP16 to make downloading them easier (since they are half the size) suddenly fail for all our users, we have a very big problem.

> Users can switch the model to fp32 if they need to.

It's not because the breaking change has a workaround that it's still a breaking change. The end user code stops working and this is something we do not want.

Thinking more about this, I don't think the model config is a good option in the end, since a user will upload a model on the Hub with a FP16 in the config and that model won't work for the inference API or all users on CPU. It should really be completely opt-in.

cc @LysandreJik and @patrickvonplaten

So how about this:

1. plan to automate this in v5 and meanwhile do the right thing only if it's triggered manually via the new `torch_dtype` arg in `from_pretrained()` / `from_config()`

body:
Your suggestions are really great! It's really nice to have an example of T5 pre-training in FLAX.

About the training of the Unigram tokenizer, it seems to me that the unigram model will need to know the token id corresponding to the "unknow" token. I'm pretty sure that otherwise an error will be returned if the tokenizer is ever asked to encode a sentence that would contain a unicode character that it has never seen in its train set.

To the best of my knowledge, it seems that we don't have a way to declare this token "easily". In my proposal [in the point 2.b of the readme](https://github.com/yandex-research/DeDLOC/blob/main/sahajbert/tokenizer/README.md), I was proposing to make a manual change in the `tokenizer.json` file to indicate this information to the tokenizer model, which is really not ideal. I was thinking that we could add a new feature in the `t5_tokenizer_model.py` file that would automatically make this change. For that, I propose to go up to the initialization level the declaration of the special tokens in order to be able to reuse at the appropriate places (post-processor and training) the id/value mapping of the special tokens.

I've tried to make all the changes that would be implied by this feature in my next comments so that you can see what I have in mind.

 Don't hesitate to tell me if I missed something or if you have a simpler solution in mind :smile:

author: patrickvonplaten

body:
```suggestion
In JAX, most transformations (notably `jax.jit`) require functions that are transformed to be stateless so that they have no side effects. This is because any such side-effects will only be executed once when the transformed function is run during compilation and all subsequent calls of the compiled function would re-use the same side-effects of the compiled run instead of the "actual" side-effects (see [Stateful Computations in JAX](https://jax.readthedocs.io/en/latest/jax-101/07-state.html). If functions could have side-effects, it would mean that In all subsequent runs, the function would not take into account the side-effects and simply re-run the side-effects of the compiled function. As a consequence, Flax models, which are designed to work well with JAX transformations, are stateless. This means that when running a model in inference, both the inputs and the model weights are passed to the forward pass. In contrast, PyTorch model are very much stateful with the weights being stored within the model instance and the user just passing the inputs to the forward pass.
```

body:
```suggestion
Another significant difference between Flax and PyTorch models is that, we can pass the labels directly to PyTorch's forward pass to compute the loss, whereas Flax models never accept labels as an input argument. In PyTorch, gradient backpropagation is performed by simply calling `.backward()` on the computed loss which makes it very handy for the user to be able to pass the labels. In Flax however, gradient backpropagation cannot be done by simply calling `.backward()` on the loss output, but the loss function itself has to be transformed by `grad` or `value_and_grad` to return the gradients of all parameters. This transformation cannot happen under-the-hood when one passes the labels to Flax forward function, so that in Flax, we simply don't allow labels to be passed by design and force the user to implement the loss function her-/himself.

```suggestion
- the main deficiency and why this one is called "naive" MP, is that all but one GPU is idle at any given moment. So if 4 GPUs are used, it's almost identical to quadrupling the amount of memory of a single GPU, and ignoring the rest of the hardware. Plus there is the overhead of copying the data between devices. So 4x 6GB cards will be able to accommodate the same size as 1x 24GB card using naive MP, except the latter will complete the training faster, since it doesn't have the data copying overhead. But, say, if you have 40GB cards and need to fit a 45GB model you can with 4x 40GB cards (but barely because of the gradient and optimizer states)
```

body:
Yeah currently, the slow tokenizer for LayoutLMv2 will also return everything in reversed order, which, to me, doesn't make sense (but for now I've implemented it in the same way as other slow tokenizers). If this will be fixed, it will be in a separate PR.

Honestly, looking at it now, there's no point in using the slow tokenizer. `LayoutLMv2TokenizerFast` is much more handy: it will handle overflowing tokens by also adding special tokens, handle padding/truncation, etc. 

Suppose that you have an example that will result in > 512 tokens, like this one:

```
from transformers import LayoutLMv2TokenizerFast

tokenizer = LayoutLMv2TokenizerFast.from_pretrained("microsoft/layoutlmv2-base-uncased")

words = ['hello' for _ in range(600)]
boxes= [[1000,1000,1000,1000] for _ in range(600)]

encoding = tokenizer(words, boxes=boxes, padding='max_length', truncation=True, return_overflowing_tokens=True)
```

Then `encoding.input_ids` will be a list of length 2, `encoding.bbox` will also be a list of length 2, etc., and you get the `overflow_to_sample_mapping`!

Funnily enough, these two lines show that there's a bit of an issue in how the docstrings are analyzed!

This splits on `"""`, therefore obtaining the following:
```py
[...]
def clean_code(content):
    
    # Remove docstrings by splitting on ')
    content = "".join(splits[::2])
    splits = content.split("'''")
    content = "".join(splits[::2])
[...]
```
Here it used the `"""` in the comment, and was lucky to find an occurrence in the next line to which skip. It removed the following line in doing so:
```py
    splits = content.split('"""')
```

```py

import re
from contextlib import contextmanager
from pathlib import Path

def clean_code(content):
    content = "".join(splits[::2])
    splits = content.split("
```

So the issue with the approach here is whether we have other occurrences in the library where `'''` is present but not part of a docstring, and same with `"""`. I doubt that's the case, but if that were so it could prove problematic for this method.

Thanks for the PR! It looks cool, but I have big rpoblems with the names :-) 

This does not follow the logic in naming we use in PyTorch or TensorFlow. A "step" is a training step, some step along the loss function following the gradients. When applying gradient accumulation, we do a step every `gradient_accumulation` training sample. I think the logs and the variable names should be adapted to reflect that, otherwise our users will be confused that we use one convention in PyTorch/TensorFlow and another one in Flax.

body:
As I focused just on the T5 I assumed that this simplification will work well. With the T5 tokenizer the class names are tokenized as:

- entailment: ["", "en", "tail", "ment"]
- neutral: ["neutral"]
- contradiction: ["contradiction"]

There is no problem with neutral and contradiction, but the entailment string is splited into 4 subtokens. My intuition was that if the model generates the first token of entailment, the probability of generating the rest of the tokens after that should be very high.  Therefore, we could estimate the probability of generating the whole entailment string just with the probability of the first token.  Doing it in this way, we can simplify a lot the inference, but it is true that we should measure how it affects the quality of the model.

You cannot do this this way.
Dict in python are not of deterministic order so `annotation.values()` is not guaranteed to be in the correct order ('score', 'label', 'box').
Even worse, this dependency is not explicity for the reader (so anyone might want to reorder the `keys` list and incur a bug.

```python
n = len(annotations["scores"]) # We're hopeful that annotations are actually of sane outputs with the same length of every key, that's very hopeful.

```python
annotation = [{"score": raw_annotation["score"][i], "label": raw_annotation["label"][i], "box": raw_annotation["box"][i] for i in range(n)]
```
I would argue that the real culprit is the `post_process` tbh, because the output might be *unsound* (different shapes for annotations is possible). As much as possible, we want to use struct/data formats that cannot allow any discrepancy to even exist (list of Annotation, won't allow any different length, which woudl result in erroneous attribution)

Let's see if we can move this logic directly within `post_process`. It seems much more natural in terms of responsability but again, I don't know who else uses `post_process` out there, so my assumptions might be wrong.

```suggestion
                sequence = "I wanted to go running, swimming and singing."
                max_length = 5

                tokenize_sequence = tokenizer(sequence, add_special_tokens=False)

                # LEFT TRUNCATION
                tokenizer.truncation_side = "left"
                truncated_sequence_left_without_special_tokens = tokenizer(
                    sequence, max_length=max_length, truncation=True, add_special_tokens=False

                for key in tokenize_sequence.keys():

                # RIGHT TRUNCATION
                tokenizer.truncation_side = "right"
                truncated_sequence_right_without_special_tokens = tokenizer(

author: Rocketknight1

body:
Hi, I have what I believe is a working implementation! Can you try this in your code in place of the existing `torch_gather` and let me know how it performs?
```
def tf_take_along_axis(x, indices, gather_axis):
    if gather_axis < 0:
        gather_axis = tf.rank(x) + gather_axis
    
    if gather_axis != tf.rank(x) - 1:
        pre_roll = tf.rank(x) - 1 - gather_axis
        permutation = tf.roll(tf.range(tf.rank(x)), pre_roll, axis=0)
        x = tf.transpose(x, perm=permutation)
        indices = tf.transpose(indices, perm=permutation)
    else:
        pre_roll = 0
        
    flat_x = tf.reshape(x, (-1, tf.shape(x)[-1]))
    flat_indices = tf.reshape(indices, (-1, tf.shape(indices)[-1]))
    gathered = tf.gather(flat_x, flat_indices, batch_dims=1)
    gathered = tf.reshape(gathered, tf.shape(indices))
    
    if pre_roll != 0:
        permutation = tf.roll(tf.range(tf.rank(x)), -pre_roll, axis=0)
        gathered = tf.transpose(gathered, perm=permutation)
        
    return gathered
```

```suggestion
        if attention_mask is not None:
            assert batch_size > 0, "batch_size has to be defined and > 0"
            attention_mask = attention_mask.view(batch_size, -1)
            # We create a 3D attention mask from a 2D tensor mask.
            # Sizes are [batch_size, 1, 1, to_seq_length]
            # So we can broadcast to [batch_size, num_attention_heads, from_seq_length, to_seq_length]
            # this attention mask is more simple than the triangular masking of causal attention
            # used in OpenAI GPT, we just need to prepare the broadcast dimension here.
            attention_mask = attention_mask[:, None, None, :]

            # Since global_attention_mask is 1.0 for positions we want to attend and 0.0 for
            # masked positions, this operation will create a tensor which is 0.0 for
            # positions we want to attend and -10000.0 for masked positions.
            # Since we are adding it to the raw scores before the softmax, this is
            # effectively the same as removing these entirely.
            attention_mask = attention_mask.to(dtype=self.dtype)  # fp16 compatibility
            attention_mask = (1.0 - attention_mask) * -10000.0
```

body:
1. GPT-J 6B easily fits in a 16 GB GPU for inference or 32 GB GPU for tuning (at FP16). CPU inference, while slow, absolutely remains an option and it isn't hard to get a server with 32 GB of memory. And besides, just because GPT-J 6B is the only model that exists today doesn't mean that other models cannot be created in the future at different scales. This is generic model class PR, not a GPT-J 6B PR.
2. Look, we understand that you are concerned with accessibility of large models. [EleutherAI expects that those looking to use our large language models will need to find beefy hardware to run them.](https://www.eleuther.ai/faq) It is an unfortunate result of scaling, but it is something we cannot help with. You can try to do fancy optimizations and swapping weights in and out of memory but that is incompatible with the `transformers` design philosophy and out of scope for this PR. There are also many suboptimal parts of `transformers` that should be prioritized that are also outside the scope of this PR yet would solve fundamental problems with running large models like GPT-J 6B with `transformers`. It frustrates me heavily that this is the case, but we are here to add initial model support, not to optimize to perfection.
3. If you want parallelization today, use Mesh Transformer JAX. Parallelization is out of scope for this PR, and in my opinion should not be considered. It is development that I think would be better suited to after this code is merged.

@g-karthik I am sorry that Eric has been quite rude to you. That said, I largely agree with the points he has raised.

As I explain [here](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/pull/13022#issuecomment-900005434), I believe you are mistaken about the size of models and the amount of GPU required to use them.

If you would like to have the `parallelize` feature implemented, you are welcome to submit a PR either to [the source of this PR](www.github.com/stellaathena/transformers) or to the `transformers` library after this PR has been merged. As I said before, `parallelize` is an experimental feature that I do not feel comfortable implementing.

Unfortunately maintaining consistent features across models is a nightmare with `transformers` due to the strict no inheritance policy. I would love for this model (as well as `GPT-Neo`) to inherit from `GPT-2`, or even better add functionality to the `GPT-2` class to allow all of these (nearly identical) models to use the same code base. I agree with you and have lobbied for this before, but my understanding is that HF is not interested in permitting these things currently. This is a HF design question that is far outside the scope of this PR, and I encourage you to take it up with them.

body:
Thank you for this PR, @hyunwoongko 

This is a general comment to the whole effort of integrating parallelformers into transformers.

1. Let's always start with one model, review, agree and when happy replicate to the rest of models in the same PR.
2. start with more than one model if that other model is different from others and requires a special different change

This will make both the reviewing process easier and it'll be much less work for you, should changes be requested.

So to stick to this proposal please don't adjust any files but the ones that were commented on, until we all agree and then all other files can follow suite.

3. Please always paste the description of the proposed change to the PR, rather than linking to other projects, since the latter may disappear in the future and it'll be difficult to understand why a certain changes was done down the road.

As such I'm going to comment only on the first 2 uniques models.

@sgugger, a question to you this is going to be potentially very extensive process. Do you prefer a step by step process which would be easy to review / integrate - like the proposed PR, or would you rather have a massive single PR? The problem is that it'll take touching on dozens of files and I think it'd be difficult to review. To me doing it in stages is a simpler approach to all involved.
