So to try again, what I was proposing is to pick all the models that require unique handling. And once those are figured out we can replicate all the similar ones. e.g. we have some models which are 95% identical to 5-10 others.

**Alternatively, we can also take a very different approach. We can pick just one model - say T5 or GPT2 and completely port it, and then do a few more models, etc, etc.** The drawback in this approach is that it'd be more difficult to see how to generalize, but I think getting one model working sooner is more practical and we can get users to start experimenting and report flaws sooner than later. Also it'll be much easier to see that we are doing the right thing, and of course tests will be needed, and we can test right away.

body:
Sure!

1. First, we get the query and support embeddings:

```
q = self.BERT(**W_query)
S = self.BERT(**W_supports)
```

2. Next, query and supports are reshaped for further easiness of calculations. The size of query becomes `(batch_size, 1, num_tokens, embedding_size)` and the size of supports becomes `(batch_size, n_examples_per_query, num_tokens, embedding_size)`

```
# reshape from (batch_size, 384, 784) to (batch_size, 1, 384, 784)
q = q.view(q.shape[0], -1, q.shape[1], q.shape[2])

# reshape from (batch_size*n_exaples_per_entity, 384, 784) to (batch_size, n_exaples_per_entity, 384, 784)
S = S.view(q.shape[0], -1, S.shape[1], S.shape[2])
```

3. Now, for each of the support set, we take the embeddings of entity start token `([E])` and end token `([/E])` for all examples in the set.

```
s_start = S[(W_supports["input_ids"] == 30522).view(S.shape[:3])].view(S.shape[0], -1, 1, S.shape[-1])
s_end = S[(W_supports["input_ids"] == 30523).view(S.shape[:3])].view(S.shape[0], -1, 1, S.shape[-1])
```

4. Lastly, find the probability of each token in the query being the start/end token by applying the following formula from the paper. I used `einsum` because I like it. Moreover, it helped me to multiply with soft attention, which is needed in training time. Also, the unused methods `VectorSum` and `Atten` is for training time. I will add training scripts soon.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/9072075/129887980-22fdb089-79ed-49cc-ba14-d5f5bd447b5e.png)

```
p_start = torch.sum(torch.einsum("bitf,bejf->bet", q, s_start), dim=1)
p_end = torch.sum(torch.einsum("bitf,bejf->bet", q, s_end), dim=1)
```

Note 1: Simply to put, the proposed idea to find these probabilities is multiplying token level similarity with sentence level similarity as soft attention.

Note 2: The paper suggested a technique to be able to use a variable number of support examples, which I am currently not providing. I have plans to add that later too.

What do you mean exactly by "...doing it twice is asking for problems"? Here is the use case:

-> we can load both models and tokenizers with strings, *e.g.*

```python
from transformers import pipeline

pipeline("ner", model="bert-base-cased", tokenizer="bert-base-cased")
```
-> so why wouldn't we allow this for the feature extractors which are essentially the same as tokenizers just for speech? 

In short I would like to be able to run the model in the pipeline in 3 lines (just like we can do with other models):

```python
librispeech_en = load_dataset("patrickvonplaten/librispeech_asr_dummy", "clean", split="validation")
asr = pipeline("automatic-speech-recognition", model="facebook/s2t-wav2vec2-large-en-de", feature_extractor="facebook/s2t-wav2vec2-large-en-de")

translation_de = asr(librispeech_en[0]["file"])
```

I don't want to have to create the feature extractor myself - it takes much more time to look up the correct classes to load the feature extractor then just passing the string.

Also, I don't really see how we're running into problems when allowing it to use the `AutoFeatureExtractor`... IMO the `AutoFeatureExtractor` was partly implemented to be used in the pipelines - currently it's not used at all

1. Fair point - I can change it to `name.endswith("EncoderDecoderModel")` to make it more readable. Note that this `if statement` only works for Encoder Decoder models

2. To break it down a bit - we start to get more and more exotic speech seq2seq models, which means that we can now already have `input_values` and `input_features` as possible input formats/names. `generate()` usually expects `input_ids` so it's not really made for generating from `input_values` and `input_features`. However all generate functionality (whether speech-features-to-text or speech-values-to-text) has one thing in common which is that it takes encoded hidden states and starts auto-regressively generating text (It's actually the same for image captioning and text generation) -> so to make the pipeline more general, I think it makes a lot of sense to call the encoder (every seq2seq model has an encoder) and first generate the hidden_states to be fed to the cross attention layer. Now the decoder also needs the original attention mask with the hidden states (all our seq2seq models pass a `(encoder_)attention_mask` to the decoder). 
=> this is exactly what we are doing here and I don't see at all why this is a problem to be honest. We just can't leave it as it is now to make it work for both `input_values` and `input_features`
author: patrickvonplaten

body:
Also, I'm having trouble understanding what is meant by "having to maintain a dependency". That's what generate does under the hood for seq2seq:

```
input_ids, attention_mask  -> encoder_outputs = encoder(input_ids), attention_mask -> generate(encoder_outputs=encoder_outputs, attention_mask=attention_mask)
```

All I'm doing here is skipping the `input_ids, attention_mask  -> encoder_outputs = encoder(input_ids)` part because `generate()` from encoder inputs is not general enough (and shouldn't be!!!) to handle multiple different inputs. The whole idea of the big generate refactor a while back: https://discuss.huggingface.co/t/big-generate-refactor/1857 was exactly to enable use-cases such those

I haven't had a chance to set up the latest pt-nightly to test it so I will follow up on the correctness once I did that.

autocast keeps everything in the original dtype (usually fp32) and only does ops that are supported in half precision when they are called. It keeps a cache of the half-precision version of the original weights for the scope of autocast. 

Also `self.dtype` in the context you highlighted only checks the first param.

Deepspeed does it differently. it keeps weights in fp16 and uses fp32 master weights only when needed. So that's why we have those checks in the code as we have "torch.float16" then - also when we use `--fp16_full_eval`

Thank you very much for this work and this addition! It's great to have found a way to speed up the tokenization of slow tokenizers.

After all the comments that have been made, I don't have much to add. Except that after renaming the variables and adding the comments I find the method very readable and understandable! Thanks also for the information about the unreliability of `Re` for this type of method.

Regarding the breaking changes, I would just like to make sure that everyone has in mind the current behaviour and the behaviour induced by this PR. As I find examples quite informative, I'm sharing two notebooks both comparing the behaviour of the `add_tokens` method for slow and fast tokenizers: but one uses the [latest release of transformers](https://colab.research.google.com/drive/1scfWUO0GV7i1zaxvescSOD8TUSYRk6IC?usp=sharing) and the other [@Narsil branch](https://colab.research.google.com/drive/1mtLvjaU9fBhFq6VKsHd64p4GDBfNSO1_?usp=sharing).  

Initially I didn't immediately see the complexity of this task (see [this comment](https://github.com/huggingface/tokenizers/issues/772)) but in the end my opinion is that fast tokenizers offer the best API for adding tokens. Currently, fast and slow tokenizers do not behave the same and it seems to me that after this PR they will still not behave the same (but not in the same way). My concern is that the difference that would now be between slow and fast tokenizers does not seem simple to understand for a new user. What do you think?

body:
```suggestion
ByT5's architecture is based on the T5v1.1 model, so one can refer to :doc:`T5v1.1's documentation page <t5v1.1>`. In contrast to T5v1.1, ByT5 is a *tokenizer-free* model meaning that it operates directly on characters/bytes whereas T5v1.1 expects subwords or tokens as an input. This has the following consequences:

- ByT5 procceses an input string of, *e.g.*, 15 characters/bytes `"my name is mary"` to 15 input ids, whereas T5v1.1 processes the same input string to just 5 input ids. As a consequence ByT5 models much longer input sequences and is thus has a higher computational cost given the same architecture and same inputs as T5v1.1
- ByT5 usually uses much fewer decoder layers than encoder layers, *e.g.* ["google/byt5-small"](https://huggingface.co/google/byt5-small) consists of 12 encoder layers, but only 4 decoder layers. This is because generating output tokens requires just a single encoder forward pass, but multiple decoder passes, therefore reducing the number of decoder layers has a much more significant impact on reducing computational cost than reducing encoder layers. T5v1.1 uses the same number of encoder - and decoder layers.
```

=> Overall I'm not really sure it's a good idea to state actual numbers like 1024 and 128 here. Especially the `max_target_length` strongly depends on the dataset. E.g. if one would train T5 on extreme summarization like XSum: https://huggingface.co/datasets/xsum 128 is not a good max target length. If one has a lot of memory and wants to try T5 on long-range summarization 128 is also not a good max target length...=> so I would rather leave the numbers out here and instead write something like:

Depending on the dataset T5 is fine-tuned on, one should carefully select :obj:`max_source_length` and :obj:`max_target_length`. 

Max source length default to 512 in T5 I think and the target length should always be carefully chosen depending on the dataset IMO - there is no golden number I think. 
So maybe we can write here that if `padding="longest"` the max_source_length usually just makes sure that the model doesn't OOM and if padding="max_length" padding/truncation is applied.
The target length has to be picked by the user depending on the task IMO

body:
The current philosophy is that for all PyTorch, TF and Flax we use -100 to pad the loss - see: https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/blob/a3f96f366a49bbe2cbdeaebd2e32ccdc1260a1d6/src/transformers/modeling_tf_utils.py#L159 and https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/blob/a3f96f366a49bbe2cbdeaebd2e32ccdc1260a1d6/examples/flax/language-modeling/run_mlm_flax.py#L228 

In Flax's summarization script we didn't follow this 1-to-1 and just pad tokens from the padding mask, which I think is fine.

The big difference between TF, Pytorch vs. Flax is that in PyTorch and TF the loss is calculated in the forward pass of the model which means that `labels` are passed to the model and they already need to have a -100 in them. In Flax, we will always compute the loss outside of the forward function which gives us more freedom and we can show in the examples that one can just not compute the loss the padding tokens - no `-100` needed in this case.

So maybe we can just leave as it is but say:

`In PyTorch and Tensorflow, ...`?
author: patrickvonplaten

Hmm, wouldn't 100% agree here - IMO it sometimes also make sense to use `pad_to_max_length` here to say put all batches in 8 buckets of different length if the input and output lengths are very different, *e.g.* for summarization.

```suggestion
- If training on TPU, it is recommended to pad all examples of the dataset to the same length or make use of `pad_to_multiple_of` to have a small number of predefined bucket sizes to fit all examples in. Dynamically padding batches to the longest example is not recommended on TPU as it triggers a recompilation for every batch shape that is encountered during training thus significantly slowing down the training.
```

body:
It's somewhat complex to achieve this for the following reasons:

1. REALM is solely a pre-training method which doesn't contain fine-tuning and predicting methods in its github codebase. The fine-tuning method and predictor are resided in *ORQA* ([paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.00300) and [codebase](https://github.com/google-research/language/tree/master/language/orqa)). Thus, we need to add another model *ORQA* to achieve this.
2. REALM's knowledge retrieving method is somehow like Deep Q Learning does, called `Asynchronous Maximum Inner Product Search (MIPS)`. In other words, it first retrieves top-K probability documents from the corpus to calculate marginal loss; then, after these retrieved documents have slightly staled, a new retrieval starts again. Therefore, I believe these steps need files of script to complete, so we might not be able to do this in the test.
3. Another way that prevents the complex process mentioned above is directly use pre-trained evidence-block (retrieved documents represented as a (num_block_records, retriever_proj_size) shape tensor), but the model function of this is also placed in *ORQA*.

Therefore, I think that we eventually need to add `ORQA` in order to achieve real end-to-end prediction, and this might be difficult to be written in the integration test.

body:
Hey @qqaatw, 

We have quite a strict policy in `transformers` that all fine-tuned models will always only be in one model checkpoint file. There is no exception to it. One of the main reasons for this is that otherwise one could not save the whole model in a single model repo (since we would need 2 `pytorch_model.bin` files) and this is sadly a no-go.

I've done the final modifications to the structure of `RealmForOpenQA` that allow to load a single checkpoint file. This has a couple of other upsides:
- we can delete the specific `from_pretrained(...)` and `save_pretrained(...)` methods
- We can add the `init_weights()` correctly under the model
- the model has now the exact same structure than RAG which is very helpful for downstream libraries such as https://github.com/deepset-ai/haystack 

Regarding the potential downsides:
- I don't fully agree that is it not intuitive to load everything in one checkpoint file. Note that we can do the exact same thing (one checkpoint) for TF later on. 
- Also we now have three main components when using RAG:
  - RagEmbedder (embeds the questions)
  - RagRetriever (which is now similar to RAG framework independent as there is no need to rely on a framework like PyTorch for an external database and which is responsible for retrieving the context to produce an answer)
  - RagReader (which reads the context and question embeddings and finds the correct index to produce the answer.
=> I think this architecture is quite intuitive and can be understood when compared to the diagram of the official paper: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2002.08909.pdf

What do you think?
author: patrickvonplaten

```python
model_id = "qqaatw/realm-open-qa"

tokenizer = RealmTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id)
retriever = RealmRetriever.from_pretrained(model_id)

model = RealmForOpenQA.from_pretrained(model_id, retriever)

predicted_answer = tokenizer.decode(predicted_answer_ids)
```

@patrickvonplaten - The `block_emb` was intended to not be a parameter because it should not participate in gradient calculations; otherwise, this would contribute to a huge memory cost especially when running on GPUs. I instead registered it as a buffer in order to save it with other parameters into a checkpoint.

```python
        self.register_buffer(
            "block_emb",
            torch.zeros(()).new_empty(
                size=(config.num_block_records, config.retriever_proj_size),
                dtype=torch.FloatTensor,
                device=torch.device("cpu"),
            ),
        )
```

Here is the original TF impl. which uses a local variable to store this tensor and doesn't save it along with other parameters.

https://github.com/google-research/language/blob/master/language/orqa/utils/scann_utils.py#L39-L64

I think the `block_emb` should always be set deterministically? otherwise the `ForOpenQA` model would become useless if the `block_emb` is initialized randomly as the retrieval process relies on this pre-computed tensor to retrieve answer contexts from the `block_records`.

body:
@patrickvonplaten The reason of requiring max-length padding strategy is that a single input would include many candidates. In the following example, a sample has two candidates, and there are two samples that subsume into a batch. The goal of this function is to produce an encoded output with `(batch_size, num_candidates, max_length)` shape for `RealmScorer`.

```
# batch_size = 2, num_candidates = 2
batch_texts = [
    ["Hello world!", "Nice to meet you!"], # First sample
    ["The cute cat.", "The adorable dog."]  # Second sample
]

tokenized_texts = tokenizer.batch_encode_candidates(text, max_length=10, return_tensors="pt")

print(tokenized_texts.input_ids.shape) # (2, 2, 10)
```

Therefore, if we don't adopt the max-length strategy and use the longest strategy instead, based on the current logic of `batch_encode_candidates`, the first sample will be firstly inputted into `__call__` and result in an output with shape (num_candidates, longest_length_of_first_sample). Then, we do the same step for the second sample and get an output with shape (num_candidates, longest_length_of_second_sample). These two outputs cannot be stacked into a batch tensor because their dimension on the last axis is different. We could however design a more sophisticated logic to adapt the longest strategy (I can do it in this PR or in a follow-up PR).

@patrickvonplaten, @patil-suraj - This function could be integrated into `__call__`, but IMO I think keeping a separated function would be more clear and unequivocal to users i.e. using `batch_encode_candidates` when they want to encode samples containing candidates for `RealmScorer`; otherwise, using the regular `__call__` to encode.

body:
Its not explicitly mentioned in the docs. But the tutorial link you sent shows the config for Bert, and that does not specify the static dimension in the output (the 768 dimension in "last_hidden_state" and "pooler_output"). So I went through the code in src/transformers/onnx to verify this. The dimensions returned by the config file are passed on to the export function provided by PyTorch in the torch.onnx module as shown in src/transformers/onnx/convert.py:

```
    export(
        model,
        (model_inputs,),
        f=output.as_posix(),
        input_names=list(config.inputs.keys()),
        output_names=onnx_outputs,
        dynamic_axes={name: axes for name, axes in chain(config.inputs.items(), config.outputs.items())},
        do_constant_folding=True,
        use_external_data_format=config.use_external_data_format(model.num_parameters()),
        enable_onnx_checker=True,
        opset_version=opset,
    )

```
As you can see, the shapes provided by the config file are passed to the dynamic_axes parameter in the function call.

I also verified the change by converting a LayoutLM model to ONNX- the verification step that runs during conversion confirmed that the outputs of the converted model are similar to the original. Visualizing the converted ONNX model using Netron also shows that the input and output sizes are as follows:

```
Inputs:     
------     
name: input_ids    
type: int64[batch,sequence]    
    
name: bbox    
type: int64[batch,sequence,4]    
    
name: attention_mask    
type: int64[batch,sequence]    
    
name: token_type_ids    
type: int64[batch,sequence]    
    
Outputs:     
-------     
name: last_hidden_state    
type: float32[batch,sequence,768]    
    
name: pooler_output    
type: float32[batch,768]
```

I do think that this should be explicitly mentioned in the docs though, so that it will be easier for anyone trying to convert custom models.

body:
The only issue I'm seeing with this method is that it has side effects on the pipeline state, which is surprising in some cases (e.g., on `__call__`).

For example here:
```py
>>> pp = pipeline("text-generation", max_length=2)
```
You would expect all generations coming from this pipeline to have a `max_length` of 2. And this works well.

When using the same pipeline for inference, with a `max_length` override, this too works as one would expect:
```py
>>> pp(["ok", "nice"], max_length=8)
Setting `pad_token_id` to `eos_token_id`:50256 for open-end generation.
Setting `pad_token_id` to `eos_token_id`:50256 for open-end generation.
[[{'generated_text': 'ok\n\nAce is my friend'}], [{'generated_text': "nice will always tell you, 'I"}]
```

What is unexpected is that now the default max length changed to 8; when this should IMO be an override and not set:

```py
>>> pp(["ok", "nice"])
Setting `pad_token_id` to `eos_token_id`:50256 for open-end generation.
Setting `pad_token_id` to `eos_token_id`:50256 for open-end generation.
[[{'generated_text': 'ok and Aarhus in Copenhagen.'}], [{'generated_text': 'nice for a while at first. I'}]
```

body:
`forward` should be called. It's just that `forward` is defined in `base` vs subclasses, just because of the `ensure_on_device` + `no_grad` wrappers that are important.

`_forward` on the other hand does not contain those guards.

`preprocess` > `forward` > `postprocess` : valid and recommended
`preprocess` > `_forward` > `postprocess` : valid but slower (no grad guards) + no GPU out of the box. (Important to keep readability within pipeline to a max.)

I think we're not going to be able to dodge the 

`if task in ...   ` to see if we need to load tokenizer or not.
It's magic, but in the correct place, so I think it's OK, but we do need a good comment explaining the rationale (why do we have a switch here and we cannot do without.)

The other idea I have would be to be OK failing to load a tokenizer a simply continue with a None value. However I think it's much worse that `if task in` because it will force downstream code to handle a new case (you won't be able to know ahead if a tokenizer was loaded properly or not, hiding any file issues)

The dummy tokenizer is a nice workaround, but very unfriendly for users.

body:
Actually, let's please not change it to `None`. If we change it to None it is created later down the road anyway so we don't gain anything from not creating it. The advantage of leaving it as `jnp.ones((batch_size, sequence_length))` is that the TPU XLA compiler knows as soon as possible what shape this variable has and can better optimize. Also passing None can lead to some problems when jitting the model.

In Flax/JAX, we only want to pass `None` for non-tensor function inputs. For all tensor function inputs we should always pass a tensor and not None.
author: patrickvonplaten

body: OK!
author: ydshieh

body:
@NielsRogge @ydshieh 

As a good rule for Flax/JAX is:

All Flax...Module that inherit from `flax.linen.Module` should **always** require to be passed each tensor argument of their call method. This means, *i.e.* that it's ok to see:

```python
def __call__(
    self, 
    hidden_states: jnp.ndarray,
    output_attentions: Optional[bool] = None,
    ...
)
```

but we don't want to see:

```python
def __call__(
    self, 
    hidden_states: Optional[jnp.ndarray] = None,
    output_attentions: Optional[bool] = None,
    ...
)
```

in the `flax.linen.Module`.

In the `Flax...Model` class this is ok since it's not a `linen.Module` that will be jitted. However inside the `Flax...Model` we should always pass tensors to its attached `linen.Module` class (each `Flax...Model` has a `self.module` property).

In the case above, the `linen.Module` class of the Decoder of FlaxVisionEncoderDecoder should except to get a `encoder_attention_mask` and not None, so let's not pass `None` in this case. We can leave a nice comment like:

```
# make sure encoder_attention_mask for decoder is always initialized to 1 since encoder does not use an attention_mask
```

Also cc @patil-suraj to hear his opinion.
author: patrickvonplaten

body:
@patrickvonplaten Thanks for the information. I have this idea intuitively when I copied the code from other Flax models.

BTW (just for the record), when the tensor arguments are really optional (because models can be used with/without cross-attention, or another arguments like `token_type_ids` or `position_ids`), they are currently being `encoder_attention_mask: Optional[jnp.ndarray] = None,`, for example

https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/blob/a14d62b0b11e6cb0c64059606e4f8dbf78e40e41/src/transformers/models/gpt2/modeling_flax_gpt2.py#L591-L598
or
https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/blob/a14d62b0b11e6cb0c64059606e4f8dbf78e40e41/src/transformers/models/bert/modeling_flax_bert.py#L624-L630

So in this case, the decoder (say `FlaxGPT2Module`) actually expect `encoder_attention_mask: Optional[jnp.ndarray] = None,`.

I can still set it to `1s` in `FlaxVisionEncoderDecoderModule` though

(`FlaxGPT2Attention` actually doesn't create `attention_mask`)

Indeed! Thank you! Plus I had a suggestion from @cbalioglu, so the 2 possible solutions are:

```
            if matched:
                p = getattr(m, split_name[0])
                def selective_to_meta(t):
                    return t.to("meta") if t is p else t
                m._apply(selective_to_meta)
```
or:
```
            if matched:
                new_val = getattr(m, split_name[0])
                if isinstance(new_val, torch.nn.Parameter):
                    # isinstance returns False for Params on meta device
                    new_val = torch.nn.Parameter(new_val.to("meta"))
                else:
                    new_val = new_val.to("meta")
                setattr(m, split_name[0], new_val)
```

The latter seems to be easier to understand for users and is slightly more efficient, since it doesn't loop over all members of the submodule, when only one is needed.

body:
I got your point. However, `tokenizer.add_special_tokens` method is only appropriate to test tokens expected to exist in `additional_special_token`. The method #13483 used is directly calling `tokenizer.add_tokens(token, special_tokens=True)` to add new special tokens, and the tokens added through this method will never occur in `tokenizer.all_special_tokens`. That's why we need this fix and the test.

TL;DR, I think we can use `tokenizer.add_special_tokens` to test whether special tokens stored in `tokenizer.all_special_tokens` can properly be tokenized, and, use `tokenizer.add_tokens` to test whether special tokens stored in `tokenizer.unique_no_split_tokens` can properly be tokenized.

What do you think?

Unless I am mistaken, it seems to me that the length of the list given as an argument to `boxes` must be the same length as the first list which corresponds to a list of words. If this is the case, it seems to me that what you have proposed will give 
```
output_txt = "'what s his name a weird test lowest'"
output_txt_list = ['what', 's', 'his', 'name', 'a', 'weird', 'test', 'lowest']

len(output_txt_list) = 8
len(len(output_txt) * [[1, 1, 1, 1]]) = 35 <- instead of 8
```
I think we should rather replace `len(output_txt) * [[1, 1, 1, 1]]` by `len(output_txt_list) * [[1, 1, 1, 1]]`.

So I propose to rewrite the end of the method in the following way in order to:
- have the same length of list for `words` and `boxes`
- use the same variable names as those used elsewhere in layoutlmv2 (`words` and `boxes)
- reorder the output of the method to put side by side words and boxes which form a kind of pair
- change the boxes in order to have a unique box per word (that could be useful to detect if we have an ordering problem)

```suggestion
        words = output_txt.split(" ")
        boxes = [[i, i, i, i] for i in range(len(words))]
        output_ids = tokenizer.encode(
            output_txt_list, boxes=boxes, add_special_tokens=False
        )

        return words, boxes, output_ids
```

body:
We don't know which parts need to be debugged ahead of time, hence everything is prepared for the developer in the various places. and a single on/off logger usually is too much information. 

The Deepspeed framework has a ton of these and they sometimes have these commented out, but most of the time they use a helper debug print util where they have a flag `force` which is `False` by default, so the code is normal but it doesn't do anything unless the developer modifies the flag to `True`.

```
print_rank0("some debug/trace", force=False)
```

Would be happy to adopt this approach at `transformers` if it resonates better. But then we need to create such a convenience function (in another PR perhaps).

Also, this is similar to:

```
        # keep for quick debug
        # print(" ".join([f"\nPYTHONPATH={self.src_dir_str}"] + cmd)); die
        execute_subprocess_async(cmd, env=self.get_env())
```

I have in various extended tests, and I use it quite often, but only when I need to. And I want the process to abort at that point, hence the `die` trigger (from Perl where it's actually a built-in function but works for python as well as it's just a random undefined symbol there). The commented out code saves a ton of time and I use it quite often when debugging these tests.

body:
Not a serious issue but for information:
I recently noticed this issue in some flax models. The `dtype` in flax models specifies the `dtype` of computation and if it's passed to a module then the computation of that module happens in that `dtype` and the return type is also the given `dtype`.

This should be handled here. Right now, if we pass `dtype=jnp.bfloat16` then the type of `embeddings` will be `bf16`, but the `cls_tokens`, `mask_tokens` and `position_embeddings` params are in `fp32`, which will change the type of `embeddings` and the computation will be done in fp32 and also the return type will be `fp32`. This makes it hard to understand the flow of dtypes

This is confusing, because if the user has passed `dtype=jnp.bfloat16` then he would expect that the computation will be done in `bf16` but it's actually happening in `fp32`.

cc @patrickvonplaten 

```suggestion
        embeddings = self.patch_embeddings(pixel_values)
        batch_size, seq_len, _ = embeddings.shape

        cls_tokens = jnp.broadcast_to(self.cls_token, (batch_size, 1, self.config.hidden_size))
        cls_tokens = cls_tokens.astype(embeddings.dtype)

        if bool_masked_pos is not None:
            mask_tokens = jnp.broadcast_to(self.mask_token, (batch_size, seq_len, self.config.hidden_size))
            mask_tokens = mask_tokens.astype(embeddings.dtype)
            # replace the masked visual tokens by mask_tokens
            w = jnp.expand_dims(bool_masked_pos, axis=-1)
            embeddings = embeddings * (1 - w) + mask_tokens * w

        embeddings = jnp.concatenate((cls_tokens, embeddings), axis=1)

        if self.config.use_absolute_position_embeddings:
            embeddings = embeddings + self.position_embeddings.astype(embeddings.dtype)

        embeddings = self.dropout(embeddings, deterministic=deterministic)
        return embeddings
```

This is a difficult question because of the word embedding just-do-it precedent. Did we have any complaints about that in the recent history?

Probably the most clean approach would be to:

1. sinusoidal - do it unconditionally
2. learned - introduce a new `--resize_position_embeddings` flag that will be tri-state 
- None (default) - do it and issue a warning that suggests to use  `--resize_position_embeddings` to explicitly control the behavior
- True: do it and issue no warning (for those of us who want to act on the warnings)
- False:  throw exception as the subsequent code will fail 

I hope this proposal isn't too complicated.

body:
See, that's where we educate users to ignore warnings, which then defeats the purpose of warnings.

I think there needs to be a way to deal with the warning so it's no longer there should a user choose to have no warnings.

So, given your commentary of not being able to easily tell the type of the embedding, my updated proposal is then:

regardless of the type of the embedding - introduce a new `--resize_position_embeddings` flag that will be tri-state 
- None (default) - do it and issue a warning that suggests to use  `--resize_position_embeddings` to explicitly control the behavior
- True: do it and issue no warning (for those of us who want to act on the warnings)
- False:  throw exception as the subsequent code will fail 

I know I'm asking you to do more work than you believe is needed - so to support my proposition - would you like me to work on that part if others agree it's important?

I'm also fine to let it go if the others feel it's hair splitting.

@siddk would you mind explaining why this is an option? The only place I've seen something similar before is in https://github.com/NVIDIA/Megatron-LM/blob/e156d2fea7fc5c98e645f7742eb86b643956d840/megatron/model/transformer.py#L157-L158 but it gets renormalized in `FusedScaleMaskSoftmax`. Effectively what I believe Megatron-LM does is
```
softmax ( QV / sqrt(d) / layer_id * layer_id)
```
What I believe this PR to be doing:
```
softmax( QV / sqrt(d) / layer_id)
```

I believe the idea behind the `/ layer_id * layer_id` trick is linked to fp16. In order to not overflow the matrix multiplication you divide by `layer_id` and since attention is done in fp32 you can remultiply by `layer_id`. So effectively it should be the same implementation as the original `GPT-2` no?
author: thomasw21

body:
Yeah so this was inspired by the Megatron code - the dividing by layer index was a heuristic to prevent overflow in FP16, which we ran into a few times training the Mistral GPT-2 small and medium models.

The `baddbmm` in the lines below actually applies the scaling value to the keys prior to the QK multiply. We chose not to re-multiply by layer_idx -- it changes the semantics a bit, but doesn't affect performance.

body:
@sgugger 
> This is a very weird edge case but since texts will be lowercased, the special tokens added in fast tokenizers should be lowercased as well or they will never be identified in texts.

I think that currently with the fast tokenizers it would be necessary to wrap it into an `AddedToken` and set the `normalized` argument to `False` so that the special token is added to the tokenizer and well detected during the tokenization if it is present in the initial text. 

The difference with the slow tokenizer is that it will make the match before the normalization and the decoded output will not be the same. For example:
```python
special_token =  '[SPECIAL TOKEN]'
tokenizer_fast = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-uncased") <- it has do_lower_case=True
tokenizer_slow = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-uncased", use_fast=False)  <- it has do_lower_case=True

tokenizer_fast.add_tokens(AddedToken(special_token, normalized=False))
tokenizer_slow.add_tokens(special_token)

print(tokenizer_fast.convert_ids_to_tokens(tokenizer_fast.encode(special_token)))
print(tokenizer_slow.convert_ids_to_tokens(tokenizer_slow.encode(special_token)))
```
will output:
```
['[CLS]', '[SPECIAL TOKEN]', '[SEP]']  <- Upper cased but only one token for the special token
['[CLS]', '[special token]', '[SEP]'] <- Lower cased
```

I think the problem is the top model with a classification head sends those arguments to the base model, which then triggers the warnings. I'm not sure just removing the warnings is the right solution since there is a modification of the kwargs that is operated. I see several potential solutions:
1. remove the warnings and the modification of the kwargs and let the user deal with the error they get (if any). If there is no error at all and this code wasn't necessary in the first place, that would be my first choice.

2. only check the parameters from the top model, and not the base model. This is could be done by adding a private kwarg to flag that to the input processing function, but this is not ideal since it would need updating all models signatures. Another way can be to use a private attribute of the model class that the model with head would set to False in the base model it uses.

loss    = rank0: 2.33 average: 2.30

body:
We should change this here. If we change the fetaure extractor config by passing `return_attention_mask=True` then we also have to save the feature extractor with the config having `return_attention_mask=True`. Otherwise people will train: https://huggingface.co/facebook/wav2vec2-base/blob/main/preprocessor_config.json (which has `return_attention_mask==False`), not save it and use the model with the default feature extractor which will lead to incorrect results. 

The problem with wav2vec2-base is that batched inference != non-batched inference by model design. In my experiments of wav2vec2-base on ASR, I found that not using the attention mask led to better results. 
Think we have to options here:

1) Not pass `return_attention_mask=True` - we would probably have to quickly re-run the experiments to see if the results are good with this as well

2) Save the feature extractor alongside the model

I don't think the trainer automatically saves the model actually.

body:
I did not train a sentencepiece for Vietnamese. 
BARTpho-syllable employs the existing pre-trained "sentencepiece" model from XLMRoBERTaTokenizer, and this pre-trained model is referred to as a vocab of 250K types. 
`reduced_vocab_file` is a vocab containing 40K Vietnamese-focused types extracted from the XLMRoBERTaTokenizer vocab of 250K types. 
Other languages can thus simply reuse BartphoTokenizer with their own `reduced_vocab_file`.
author: datquocnguyen

body:
No, it will not. BartphoTokenizer is used for `bartpho-syllable` only. 

`barpho-word` employs PhobertTokenizer, as shown in its `config.json` file and our paper: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2109.09701.pdf

The difference between `bartpho-syllable` and `bartpho-word` is that they take different types of input texts: syllable level for `bartpho-syllable` (e.g. 7-syllable written text “chúng tôi là những nghiên cứu viên”) vs. word level for `barpho-word` (e.g. 4-word text “chúng_tôi là những nghiên_cứu_viên”). So they use different tokenizers.
author: datquocnguyen

body:
Is this necessary? I am not sure.
This M2M100Tokenizer has an opposite operating manner compared to ours. M2M100Tokenizer is multilingual,  allowing to add extra types.
Ours, on the other hand, is a monolingual, to reduce the size of an existing/pre-trained multilingual vocab (e.g. equivalent to reducing model sizes of XLM-RoBERTa or mBART when working with only Vietnamese).

body:
Thanks for the review! 
It's true that `past_key_values`  is never used in the encoder. And this is already ensured by the `forward()` in T5ForConditionalGeneration:
https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/blob/9e5fa33cdc5fb596bdf08b88aadf9e0b551a5b76/src/transformers/models/t5/modeling_t5.py#L1571-L1579
So, I think it's unnecessary to double-check this in T5Block, which is the case in BART.

As for the purpose of using `past_key_values `in the encoder, some research uses it to enrich the context for the input sequence. And according to my experiments in BART model, this actually works.
And in BARTForConditionalGeneration, though the `past_key_values` is not used in the encoder, it can be done by explicitly calling the `BARTEncoder(past_key_values=xxx,` **kwargs), and then pass the `encoder_outputs` to BART.

Therefore, I hope we can remove this `assert` in the T5 model as well.

By the way, if this `assert` is deleted, we should also change the following code to `past_key_values[-2:]` to avoid IndexError in the encoder because the length of  `past_key_values` ' is 2 for self-attention.
https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/blob/7db2a79b387fd862ffb0af72f7148e6371339c7f/src/transformers/models/t5/modeling_t5.py#L635

body:
I really like the clarity of the docstring here.

~~Why don't we just put `id`, `label` and `score` directly within the dict instead of creating `segments_info`?~~

I am not a big fan of `png_string` as a name as it does not really describe the content, which is the actual segmentation. It does convey the format correctly so it's good in that sense.
Maybe naming is `segmentation_mask` would be better ? It does convey that it's a `segmentation` output, so the semantic meaning of the value. Also the `mask` aspect adds that's it will contain integer values that have to be interpreted as categories instead of real RGB values. `mask` tend to be only 0 or 1 so it's a bit misleading here and we're loosing the fact that it's a base64 encoded thing. Any ideas for an even better name ?

If we actually move to masks, we can remove the nesting of `segments_info`. Payload is going to be increased but that's OK IMO as pipelines are supposed to make things easy (nesting is making things harder IMO)

You're actually loosing representation power by using a single `png_string` for output as a single pixel can now only belong in 1 mask. For `part-aware` it seems to me that pixels of a wheel should be both tagged as `car` and `wheel` (with `wheel` belonging in `car`).

If you're using real masks, then that issue will be gone.

Also PNG format should be a implementation detail, we shouldn't rely on it too heavily on it (so leaving out of the name seems a bit better IMO)
author: Narsil

body:
Never use for loops in tests. Or very exceptionally.
Never use inner functions in tests.

Both really hurt the main asset of a test, which is readability. A reader needs to be able to read a single test and know if it's valid or not, with as little as possible surrounding context.

Here, reader needs to understand what variable is sent to `test_outputs`, understand the function itself, then reason if variable was supposed to be A, [A] or something else to assess if the test is correct.


```python
outputs = image_segmenter("./tests/fixtures/tests_samples/COCO/000000039769.png", threshold=0.0)
self.assertEqual(nested_simply(outputs, {.....})

# Easy to read that if input is list, output is list.
outputs = image_segmenter(["./tests/fixtures/tests_samples/COCO/000000039769.png"], threshold=0.0)
self.assertEqual(nested_simply(outputs, [{.....}])

outputs = image_segmenter("./tests/fixtures/tests_samples/COCO/000000039769.png", threshold=0.0, subtask="panoptic")
self.assertEqual(nested_simply(outputs, {.....})

....
```

More details:
This output shape
```py
List(Dict(
    mask: str, // base64 str
    label: float,
    score: int,
    parent: int // -1 for all for DetrForSegmentation
))
```
will allow us to implement `part-aware panoptic` segmentation (which is the most detailed segmentation subtask). And  using this output, a user can re-construct `semantic`, `instance` or any othre segmentation subtask if they want

body:
For this particular example of 

> Hub model checkpoint -> ONNX -> ONNX Runtime

the code is identical for PyTorch and TensorFlow because `transformers.onnx` automatically detects which framework the model weights are loaded in. And once you have the ONNX model, you're free to choose which accelerator to run it on.

What we could do is explicitly load and save a TensorFlow model with e.g. 

```python
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, TFAutoModelForSequenceClassification

# Load tokenizer and TensorFlow model form the Hub
tokenizer = tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("distilbert-base-uncased")
tf_model = TFAutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("distilbert-base-uncased")
# Save to disk
tokenizer.save_pretrained("local-tf-checkpoint")
tf_model.save_pretrained("local-tf-checkpoint")
# Export TensorFlow checkpoint to ONNX
python -m transformers.onnx --model=local-tf-checkpoint onnx/
```

This has the nice feature of showing what's needed to export a local model.

@Albertobegue I realise this has been a long PR, so I'm happy to take care of this detail in a separate PR if you want :)

body:
This was quite important to stabilize Wav2Vec2 pre-training and it's due to the fact that vanilla PyTorch DDP simply averages all gradients over all devices even though the gradients on each device can have very much different importances. E.g. if my gradients on device 1 were computed with 200 losses but on device 2 with just 20 then the gradients on device 1 should have 10 times more weight than the gradients on device 2. In this example script it is solved as follows:

- 1. sum the losses on each device instead of averaging and compute gradient on each device
- 2. sum losses over all devices
- 3. multiply DDP-averaged gradients afterwards with num_devices / num_total_losses

=> not doing this led to unstable / breaking training. Fairseq also has this "correct" gradient averaging implemented here: https://github.com/pytorch/fairseq/blob/dd3bd3c0497ae9a7ae7364404a6b0a4c501780b3/fairseq/trainer.py#L844

We don't have this functionality in `Trainer` as far as I'm aware and I don't think it's always needed as usually the number of losses per device is more or less the same. However, in the case of speech-pretraining this can lead to huge differences, *i.e.* 
- We can't blockify the speech inputs and audio files have very different noise backgrounds -> therefore we end up with samples as long as 20 seconds and others only of length 2 seconds with neither 2 seconds nor 20 sections being exceptions. 
- The large model can only fit batch_size 1-4 per device so that the samples can't really "average each other out" on each device
=> therefore it's quite important to correctly scale the gradients afterward

I could see similar problems in long-range summarization and other NLP tasks... @sgugger, @stas00 do you guys think we should/could support this natively in Trainer somehow or is it even desired? Maybe we should leave a note in the docs no? 

@stas00 - would it be easy to implement the gradient averaging in `deepspeed` as well? How should it be handled there?

Nope, `tf.cast` coerces both python numpy values into a Tensor here whereas `tf.convert_to_tensor` only does this for numpy arrays:

```
>>> tf.cast([0, 1, 0, 1], dtype=tf.bool)
<tf.Tensor: shape=(4,), dtype=bool, numpy=array([False,  True, False,  True])>
>>> tf.cast(np.array([0, 1, 0, 1]), dtype=tf.bool)
<tf.Tensor: shape=(4,), dtype=bool, numpy=array([False,  True, False,  True])>
```

This behavior is also tested with whatever the default tokenizer `return_tensors` is (looks like they are just lists)

body:
I don't understand really - users of `greedy` and `sample` can just `MaxLengthCriteria` - it's exactly the same as `MaxNewTokensCriteria` only that `max_length = start_length + max_new_tokens`. So IMO there is zero gain in doing:

```python
start_lengths = input_ids.shape[-1]
max_new_tokens = 30

MaxNewTokensCriteria(start_length=start_length, max_new_tokens=max_new_tokens)
```

over

```python
max_length = input_ids.shape[-1] + max_new_tokens

MaxLengthCriteria(max_length=max_length)
```

Having both logits processors is confusing and `max_length` is clearly the standard that's being used in `transformes`. Also given that `max_length` is an input to `sample` and `greedy` it's much more natural to think in `MaxLengthCriteria`.
It's a deprecation warning so the functionality still exist and I'd like to merge it in this PR as we essentially render `MaxNewTokensCriteria` obselete here (99% of users use `generate()`)

Users that directly call `sample` or `greedy` know `generate()` well enough to understand how `max_length` works IMO

Overall, `max_length` is the de-facto standard in all generation models and this won't change anymore. The community is used to it. I'm happy with adding a new `max_new_tokens` for `generate()` for use cases where the input_ids is of variable length and where only the actual num of tokens that are generated matters.

Moreover the slow tokenizer does not add the special token to the vocabulary if it does not exist, so if I do not miss anything this PR would add a difference of behavior between the tokenizers slows and the tokenizers fast of type Albert.

With your PR, I obtain:
```python

From my understanding of the code it seems to me that the args and kwargs arguments of the fast tokenizer are not passed to the slow tokenizer. author: SaulLu

body:
Kindly check out the following code:

https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/blob/c28bc80bbbe0cf5cb289944ec2374d5397ff6e31/src/transformers/tokenization_utils_fast.py#L104-L123

There are four ways to instantiate FastTokenizer. The first two are not applicable to this case as they are either instantiated from an existing fast tokenizer object or file i.e. The `[MASK]` token handled or not by `AlbertTokenizerFast.__init__` doesn't matter because all states have already stored in the object or file (explained below). 
The last two are instantiated from a converted slow tokenizer which handles everything (including the `[MASK]` token) in its constructor then is converted to the fast one. 

So if we start from 

`tokenizer = AlbertTokenizerFast("tests/fixtures/spiece.model")`

The running flow will be

`AlbertTokenizerFast.__init__`
`PreTrainedTokenizerFast.__init__`
`self.slow_tokenizer_class is not None (fourth condition)` 
`slow_tokenizer = self.slow_tokenizer_class(*args, **kwargs)` << Pass args & kwargs to slow tokenizer.
`fast_tokenizer = convert_slow_tokenizer(slow_tokenizer)`
`kwargs.update(slow_tokenizer.init_kwargs)` << Update FastTokenizer's kwargs from the slow one
`super().__init__(**kwargs)`
...

And, if we start from pretrained instead

`tokenizer = AlbertTokenizerFast.from_pretrained("albert-base-v2")`

The running flow will be

`AlbertTokenizerFast.__init__`
`PreTrainedTokenizerFast.__init__`
`fast_tokenizer_file is not None and not from_slow (second condition)`
`fast_tokenizer = TokenizerFast.from_file(fast_tokenizer_file)`
`super().__init__(**kwargs)`  <<The config in kwargs doesn't affect its behavior as the fast tokenizer instance was already created from the file.

So there would result in another weird behavior. That is, even though I've set `cls_token` and `bos_token` to `[MASK]`, the tokenized outputs ramain unchanged:

```
tokenizer = AlbertTokenizerFast.from_pretrained("albert-base-v2", cls_token="[MASK]", bos_token="[MASK]")
tokenized_ids = tokenizer("hello").input_ids

print(tokenizer.cls_token) # '[MASK]'
print(tokenizer.convert_ids_to_tokens(tokenized_ids)) # ['[CLS]', '▁hello', '[SEP]']
```

If you are still worried about some edge cases, I'm happy to add the line back!
author: qqaatw
SaulLu

body:
> So there would result in another weird behavior. That is, even though I've set cls_token and bos_token to [MASK], the tokenized outputs ramain unchanged:

Indeed, to actually change the special tokens added to the sequence it would be necessary to modify the tokenizer wrapped by the fast tokenizer and stored in the attribute `backend_tokenizer`. In this case, it would be necessary to modify the `PostProcessor` of the `backend_tokenizer` and for the moment it seems to me that the idea of the initialization of the fast tokenizers was rather to give to the wrapper the information already contained in the `backend_tokenizer`.

The addition of `self.sanitize_special_tokens()` is indeed diverging from this design and that's why I'm still not 100% that it's the best way to solve the problem you raised (the fact that the reloaded tokenizer after a registration is not the same anymore).

If you finally decide to adjust the workflow i.e. always sanitizing special tokens even if the special tokens do not exist in the vocab, I'm happy to open another PR for it.

body:
@Rocketknight1 Good point. Yes, it is possible. However

- The line `position_embeds = tf.tile(input=position_embeds, multiples=(input_shape[0], 1, 1))` is everywhere in TF model scripts. If we change here, probably it is better to change all (?)
- `tf.broadcast_to` is not perfect as mentioned in TF doc [broadcast_to](https://www.tensorflow.org/api_docs/python/tf/broadcast_to)

  ```
  When doing broadcasted operations such as multiplying a tensor by a scalar,
  broadcasting (usually) confers some time or space benefit, as the broadcasted
  tensor is never materialized.
  
  However, broadcast_to does not carry with it any such benefits. The newly-created
  tensor takes the full memory of the broadcasted shape. (In a graph context, broadcast_to
  might be fused to subsequent operation and then be optimized away, however.)
  ```

But after diving deeper, I found something more severe: 

The `...INPUTS_DOCSTRING` (everywhere in transformers) specifies `position_ids` should have shape `(batch_size, sequence_length)`. If a user specify `position_ids` manually with the full `batch_size` (very unlikely though), then the line `tf.tile` shouldn't be run! (otherwise the `batch_size` will become squared). 

If we use `tf.broadcast_to`, we don't have such issue.

Could you discuss with @sgugger  and @LysandreJik  to see what to do about this, please?
author: ydshieh

body:
I don't think we need `tf.broadcast_to` either - because the first dimension of `position_embeds` is 1, we can just remove the tile line entirely, and position_embeds will still be correctly broadcast in the next line. In other words, the code would just be:
```
position_embeds = tf.gather(params=self.position_embedding, indices=position_ids)
final_embeddings = inputs_embeds + position_embeds
```

I did some quick testing and this seems to work fine. However, it's just a nit, and the performance impact will likely be small anyway, so don't worry about it too much! We can also just leave it, and I'll make a note later to check the codebase for instances of `tile` that should be replaced with implicit broadcasting.
author: Rocketknight1

body: Also, thinking about it more, using broadcasting resolves your issue with the users specifying a full batch of `position_ids`, so maybe it's more than just a minor performance nit!

Sorry for the long time without review, I had somehow missed the notification for this PR.

Thanks a lot for all your work! The new example you add is very cool! There is a little bit of work to polish the PR before we can merge it but this is already in great shape! I have left a few comments, the two main things are:
- don't define a new tokenizer class since we can re-use the existing BERT tokenizers (I know some old models have subclasses but we don't do this anymore)
- use "Copied from" statements in your modeling file to keep copies from the BERT modeling files up to date (you can see examples in the RoBERTa modeling file for instance)

One last point is the new dependency added, as you mentioned. Since one cannot import the model without it, you should add a new function that checks whether the necessary modules are installed (see for instance `is_scatter_available` used for the TAPAS model) and you should only conditionally import in the main init, like it is done for TAPAS. Running `make fix-copies` will then create the appropriate file with dummy classes so we can still import something called `QDQBertModel` in the init when the dependency is not there.

And for proper testing, and doc, the line with the pip install you mention should probably be added in the config.yml file that triggers circleCI.

Let us know if you need help with any of those steps!

I guess longformer falls into the category of max_model_length > 1000 which does not have the test (since it would require creating a string so long to get out of the model bounds it's a bit too much for tests IMO).

Bart didn't seem to exhibit the same flaw. author: Narsil

body:
If `max_length` > `model_max_length` a lot of warnings/errors are triggered.

So this would actually require users to use a different `max_length` than what they would send to `generate` (since generate doesn't allow `max_length` >  `model_max_length` in TF at least).

Semantically, I think this becomes very confusing, even in tests, it would require to do clever calculations, involving knowing somehow the model capacity and the current text length in tokens (which you don't have beforehand). It also implies modifying a given argument (`max_length`) before sending it downstream to `generate` which IMHO is very bad design/ very confusing.

Using `max_new_tokens` here is the only way that's simple and declared intention unambiguously IMO.

body:
@sgugger yes it was. Actually issue lied in upstream model used for testing which incorrectly defined its tokenizer.model_max_length (since modified): https://huggingface.co/sshleifer/tiny-distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english

Here we still need this update because for pipelines tests:

- We take the tokenizer from ModelTester checkpoint
- We train a smaller tokenizer from it
- We create a random model from ModelTester.get_config (or ModelTester.get_pipeline_config)

That means the actual values between both can be out of sync (the case here) so we still need that override here.

body:
@patrickvonplaten Thanks for that remark, finding good names is important.

`truncate_left` is a bit misleading though because all methods will end up truncating left (don't think there's a way to avoid it really). The 3 options I have in mind:

- `hole`: (Truncate left a chunk equivalent to desired new tokens, run generation as usual). you might delete quite a bit of context for your generation.
- `correct_and_slow`: (Don't truncate left at the start, but disable past_values and start generating 1 token at a time without using past and truncating left one by one as you generate new tokens)
- `incorrect_and_fast`: Same as correct_and_slow but keep using past_key_values to keep same performance. It's correct on models without position embeddings (not that many I believe), and will drift on other models (if it's only a few tokens difference might be negligible.

Do you think there are other ways to handle long generation ?

I agree `hole` might be not very clear or adapted.

- `truncate_chunk_left` ?
- `truncate_block` ?


`correct_and_slow` could be... `strict` maybe (it conveys IMO the correctness of it and the fact that it's limiting in some form) of `slow` (if the other is `fast`)
`incorrect_and_fast` could be `fast`, `approximate`.

Other names could be more descriptive:

`rotate_left_no_past`
`rotate_left_keep_past`
maybe ?


BTW, the `fast`/`slow` option I don't intend to add soon, because they require more work within `generate` and don't seem as necessary for the moment, they just seem other strategies that could be valid depending on context.
